> You say that intra-cluster connections are a separate thing but it is not really clear to me if we should set a different certificate and private key for those connections respect to user connections.

What I'd like to support is (potentially) different policies for user-to-cluster (u2c) and intra-cluster (ic) communications, and that we default to the most secure communication for the ic. The reason is that we can secure the ic communication automatically without asking anything to the user, so there's no burdern to a higher level of security. Then the user may opt to use non-SSL for u2c.

Reviewing this, I suspect this would imply:
* For Citus clusters, we enable SSL by default on Postgres unless the user explicitly disables `SGShardedCluster.spec.ssl` (or equivalent).
* For Citus clusters, by default, we generate SSL certificates *per server* but all from the same CA, and then set the `citus.node_conninfo` appropriately. So we need to autogenerate a CA, and then one certificate per server, and set this configuration appropriately. Each server (which btw includes coordinators and shards) requires to access locally the CA (common to all nodes) and server (private to each node) certificate. We can set `sslmode` to `verify-ca` even though we could experiment setting the [`citus.local_hostname`](https://docs.citusdata.com/en/v11.3/develop/api_guc.html#local-hostname) parameter and try to see if we can make it work with `verify-full` (which would be ideal for an automated deployment).
* By not "touching" anything else (in `pg_hba.conf`), client connections to the cluster may use lower security settings, all the way down to even not using SSL.
* Both for the `SGCluster` as well as the `SGShardedCluster` we should allow a setting under SSL to force require SSL. This affects only `pg_hba.conf` where we don't add any `host` entry and rather `hostssl` entries. This can become a separate issue, could be post `1.5`.
* I agree with the `autoGenerate` flag for `SGCluster` (so far it won't be needed for `SGShardedCluster`, as here we need the server certificates to be all generated from the same CA). Also I'd make `autoGenerate` the default value if `SGCluster.spec.ssl` is on (which is highly desirable, less burden on the user). This can become a separate issue, could be post `1.5`, but could also be nice to add it so we don't change later the default behavior (that the certificate secrets are not required if they are autogenerated).

In reality this is a totally independent issue more related to management of `pg_hba.conf`. There is a related, but not complete, issue about this (https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/issues/1106). Probably requires a separate issue, and it's not required for `1.5` at all.

Issue:
Refactor mutating webhooks in order to generate a patch after modifying the object
Mutating webhooks is implemented using a pipeline that generates the patches to apply to the object in order to be applied by the kubernetes server API. To generate the patches the handler have to set a `JsonPointer` to the field the handler want to change and is not really a straightforward process since it have to be checked against Jackson serialization someway. Also, if some of those handlers that are called by the pipeline produces conflicting changes we need to order the pipeline someway and maintain it, sometimes bug are not encountered until the pipeline is executed in some unexpected order. To avoid those inconvenient we want to refactor the mutating webhooks in order to generate a patch after modifying the object.

## Implementation plan

Issue:
[DEV] Create a Web console user management
### Problem to solve

This issue covers the tasks of the Dev team for this epic.

Currently, the way to add new users to the StackGres web console is in a k8s way, creating secrets for users, then cluster role and cluster role bindings as it is explained here https://stackgres.io/doc/latest/api/rbac/. It would be nice to have an administration page to manage the web console users.

### Further details

As it is necessary to create roles and roles binding we can create some predefined roles like the primitive roles:

* Admin
* Editor
* Viewer

and if needed allow the users to add their own roles using access policies.

### Proposal

* Create a StackGres console user management module.

## Acceptance Criteria

* List users
* Create users
* Edit existing users
* Delete users
* List roles
* Assign primitive roles or custom roles to users
* Create new roles
* Edit existing roles

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: After talking with @gcannata I would like to introduce a proposition for this issue.

User creation should require apart from the k8sUsername (optionally the apiUsername) and password the name of the secret. When returned from the endpoint an user will be represented by the name of the secret and the k8sUsername (optionally the apiUsername) being the name of the secret the identifier. If more than one Secret for the same user exists it means that the user has an alias and / or a different password. This is the proposed model for the user:

```yaml
metadata:
  namespace: <string>
  name: <string>
k8sUsername: <string>
apiUsername: <string>
password: <string>
roles:
- namespace: <string>
  name: <string>
clusterRoles:
- name: <string>
```

The proposed endpoints for users are:

* GET `/stackgres/users` -> List users
* POST `/stackgres/users` -> Create user
* PUT `/stackgres/users` -> Update user
* DELETE `/stackgres/users` -> Delete user

The association of `ClusterRole` / `Role` to a username (AKA `k8sUsername`) will be performed when a user will be created or modified by associating the `ClusterRole` or `Role` to the user.

Creation of roles can be at cluster or namespace level and will follow the structure of the `ClusterRole` / `Role` resources of Kubernetes:

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: (ClusterRole|Role)
metadata:
  namespace: <string>
  name: <string>
roles:
- apiGroups: [<string>]
  nonResourceURLs: [<string>]
  resourceNames: [<string>]
  resources: [<string>]
  verbs: [<string>]
```

The proposed endpoints for roles are:

* GET `/stackgres/roles` -> List roles
* POST `/stackgres/roles` -> Create role
* PUT `/stackgres/roles` -> Update role
* DELETE `/stackgres/roles` -> Delete role

The proposed endpoints for clusterroles are:

* GET `/stackgres/clusterroles` -> List cluster roles
* POST `/stackgres/clusterroles` -> Create cluster role
* PUT `/stackgres/clusterroles` -> Update cluster role
* DELETE `/stackgres/clusterroles` -> Delete cluster role

The name of the `ClusterRole` and `Role` can collide with the names of existing resources so that the WebConsole should do a `dryRun` to check the name do not exists already. Also, to avoid messing with `ClusterRole`, `Role`, `ClusterRoleBinding` and `RoleBinding` that are not meant to be used by StackGres user management, the label `api.stackgres.io/auth` and value `user` will be added to `ClusterRole`, `Role`, `ClusterRoleBinding` and `RoleBinding` resources when created, updated, deleted and listed.

cc: @ldgarcia @jose_oss_pg @ahachete @jorsol @gcannata

Issue:
[DEV] Implement profile field
StackGres tries to enforce by default best practices for production workloads. For instance, this means that podAntiAffinity is set so that no more than one StackGres pod runs on the same node.

However, there are some use cases where StackGres is not used for production, and some of these settings make user's like a little bit harder.

The goal of this issue is to introduce a new configuration field in the `SGCluster` that will allow the user to easily switch between different profiles, which will select different defaults depending on this setting. Users will be able to still override the defaults of those profile's settings.

The field is proposed to be:

```
spec:  
  profile: development|production #default 'production'
```

The following parameters will have a different default depending on this setting:

* `production`: is the default profile and will match exactly the current defaults
* `testing`: Set `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disableClusterPodAntiAffinity` to `true`
* `development`: Same as `testing` plus sets `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disablePatroniResourceRequirements` and `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disableClusterResourceRequirements` both to `true`

Independently on the profile value the above settings the user will be able to overwrite them at will.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Implement the profile field

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: We know we have the following uses cases that are not covered by our current single default profile unless you set some non production options and configuration flags:

1. Run two databases in the same node in production
2. Run a database with Pod's containers that does not set limits
3. Run a database with Pod's containers that does set limits only on chosen containers
4. Run a database with Pod's containers that does not set requests
5. Run a database with Pod's containers that does set requests only on chosen containers
6. Run a database with Pod's containers that has exactly the resources limits and requests specified by the user

Based on the use cases above we could craft a series of profiles that instead of reflecting production, staging and development environment will reflect one or a combinations of the above.

This is my proposition for the `profile` field values:

* `limits-one-pod-per-node` <- current default profile
* `limits`
* `requests-one-pod-per-node` <- default profile
* `requests`
* `only-limits-one-pod-per-node`
* `only-limits`
* `one-pod-per-node`
* `free`

The above profiles proposed solve points 1, 2 and 4.

To solve 3, 5 and 6 we should always allow to change and remove limits and resources freely on any of the containers. This probably touches the context of issue #2090 but lets discuss here since we will just solve it in the implementation of this one. The proposition is to allow to set to `null` both `cpu` and `memory` in an `SGInstanceProfile` for `.spec`, `.spec.containers.<container name>`, `.spec.initContainers.<container name>`, `.spec.requests`, `.spec.requests.containers.<container name>` and `.spec.requests.initContainers.<container name>`. Also we should generate the `.spec.requests`, `.spec.requests.containers` and `.spec.requests.initContainers` with default values enough sane in order to not break the cluster too much. This two changes will allow the user to set limits and resources freely for any container. The profile instead will control if we will have to apply both limits and requests or any of the two only. In any case the `SGInstanceProfile` allow for a total control if the user requires to relax the profile (like removing any limit or request for any container).

IMHO should be the user who chose which of the above profile should be the production, staging and development profile. This depends a lot on the user needs and, as we experienced already, we should avoid setting the bar in this aspect since it will screw first user experience. So we should introduce production, staging and development profile as mere configuration setup that is only exposed in the Web Console and StackGres REST API and can be freely configured by the SGConfig CRD (probably something that can be levereaged by #2308/#2382).

WDYT?

[teoincontatto]: After the meeting discussion we reached the conclusion that the new field `SGCluster.spec.profile` will allow a set of values. Each value will change the default of other fields of the SGCluster. This will be extended in the future in order to be configurable.

The profile proposed and the field defaults are as follow:

* `production`: is the default profile and will match exactly the current defaults
* `testing`: Set `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disableClusterPodAntiAffinity` to `true`
* `development`: Same as `testing` plus sets `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disablePatroniResourceRequirements` and `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disableClusterResourceRequirements` both to `true`

Issue:
Adding sharded backup feature SGShardedBackup
The goal is to implement the backups on the SGShardedBackup.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Implement, document and test the backups for SGShardedBackup.

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: The proposal is to create a new CRD called `SGShardedBackup` that will create a Job that will set the Job name in the status, acquire the lock on the CronJob resources created to set up the scheduled backups, call the function `citus_create_restore_point` in the coordinator with the same name as the `SGShardedBackup` and will create a set of `SGBackup` (one for coordinator and one for each shard) each of which will be monitored until they completed. After the `SGBackup` are completed (failed or not) the Job will update the status with the list of `SGBackup` names, the timing and, if failed, the failure message.

Here is the proposed CRD model:

```yaml
apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1alpha1
kind: SGShardedBackup
spec:
  sgShardedBackup: <string> # The name of the `SGShardedCluster` from which this backup is/will be taken. 
                            # If this is a copy of an existing completed backup in a different namespace
                            # the value must be prefixed with the namespace of the source backup and a
                            # dot `.` (e.g. `<sharded cluster namespace>.<sharded cluster name>`) or have the same value
                            # if the source backup is also a copy.
  managedLifecycle: <boolean> # Indicate if this backup is permanent and should not be removed by the automated retention policy. Default is `false`.
status:
  process:
    failure: [<string>]   # If the status is `failed` this field will contain a list of messages indicating the
                          # failure reasons.
    jobPod: <string>      # Name of the pod assigned to the backup. StackGres utilizes internally a
                          # locking mechanism based on the pod name of the job that creates the backup.
    status: <string>      # Status of the backup.
    timing:
      start: <string>     # Start time of backup
      end: <string>       # End time of backup
      stored: <string>    # Stored time of backup
  backupInformation:
    postgresVersion: <string> # Postgres version of the server where the sharded backup is taken from.
    size:
      uncompressed: <integer> # Size (in bytes) of the uncompressed sharded backup.
      compressed: <integer> # Size (in bytes) of the compressed sharded backup.
  sgBackups: [<string>] # List of the SGBackups associated to this backup
```

Other than this we will have to introduce a new functionality in the `SGCluster` CRD in order to disable the scheduled backups. To do this the `cronSchedule` field will be optional so that if not specified will mean there will no be a CronJob for the SGCluster in order to create backups automatically. This will allow the `SGShardedCluster` to manage such aspect with its CronJob.

We will have to create also a new section in the `SGShardedCluster` in order to allow to restore the generated `SGShardedBackup`. This will be a copy of the `SGCluster.spec.initialData.restore.fromBackup` section but only including the `name` field. The recovery will set the `target_name` to the same name as the `SGShardedBackup`.

[teoincontatto]: The phases for a major version upgrade SGDbOps would then be:

* `pre-checks`: Pre-check for upgrading SGCluster to the new major version (a dry-run patch)
* `pre-upgrade`: The pre-upgrade to actually upgrade SGCluster to the new major version and set the status of the operation, wait for the operator to change the StatefulSet to include the `major-version-upgrade` init container and restart the primary Pod
* `downscale`: If needed, downscale to the primary instance only
* `checkpoint`: Double CHECKPOINTs
* `upgrade`: Wait for the primary Pod to perform the upgrade (or upgrade dry-run when `check` is `true`) and become ready
* `post-upgrade`: If the upgrade operation was successful or was not an upgrade dry-run the old data and extensions are removed from the primary PV
* `pre-rollback`: If the upgrade operation fails or was an upgrade dry-run, performs a rollback restoring the SGCluster to previous version, waiting for the operator to change the StatefulSet to include the `major-version-upgrade` init container and set the `ROLLBACK` flag to `true` and restart the primary Pod
* `rollback`: If the upgrade operation fails or was an upgrade dry-run, waits for the primary Pod to perform the rollback and become ready
* `upscale`: If needed, upscale to the initial number of instances
* `cleanup`: Cleanup the status of the operation from the SGCluster

The existing endpoint for SGCluster stats in the StackGres REST API already returns information about the total amount of, respectively, cpu and memory resources requested (but also used and found) for both all Pods together and each Pod:

pods:

[teoincontatto]: I was wondering if it makes sense to change the goal of this issue and instead of having both limits and requests calculated from the total we should split this idea into two separate calculation, one for limits and one for requests.

In terms of resources in Kubernetes what prevent the whole Pod from being scheduled is the total amount of cpu and memory requests. So it make sense to apply a subtractive calculation on those resources values so that `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.cpu` and `.spec.requests.memory` represent the total of requests by default (that can be changed using the field `SGCluster.spec.pods.resources.disableResourcesRequestsSplitFromTotal`).

OTOH, the limits prevent a single container to use more cpu or get killed to use too much memory. For limits it makes more sense to use separate values so that changing the limits of containers does not affect the limits of patroni container. There is no real reason to make the total of limits match the `SGInstanceProfile.spec.cpu` and `SGInstanceProfile.spec.memory` fields.

[teoincontatto]: The proposal is to have an SGInstanceProfile that will look as follow (simplified with just 1 container and made up values):

```yaml
kind: SGInstanceProfile
spec:
  cpu: 2
  memory: 2Gi
  containers:
    pgbouncer:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 2
    memory: 2Gi
    containers:
      pgbouncer:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
```

The above resource will be generated by this one (all other added fields above are defaults):

```yaml
kind: SGInstanceProfile
spec:
  cpu: 2
  memory: 2Gi
```

Now, the Pods that will be generated will look like so (also extremely simplified):

```yaml
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: patroni
    resources:
      limits: # limits for patroni will just copy `SGInstanceProfile.spec.cpu` and
              #  `SGInstanceProfile.spec.memory`
        cpu: 2
        memory: 2Gi
      requests: # requests for patroni will be .spec.cpu and .spec.memory minus the sum of
                #  `.resources.requests.cpu` and `.resources.requests.memory` respectively for each
                #  `Pod.spec.containers` that is not patroni.
                # if `SGCluster.spec.pods.resources.disableResourcesRequestsSplitFromTotal` is set
                #  to `true` then it will just copy `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.cpu` and
                #  `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.memory`
        cpu: 1900m
        memory: 1920Mi
  - name: pgbouncer
    resources:
      limits: # limits for other containers will just copy
              #  `SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.<container name>` but are only enabled if
              #  `SGCluster.spec.pods.resources.enableClusterLimitsRequirements` is set to `true`.
      requests: # requests for other containers will just copy
                #  `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.containers.<container name>`
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
```

Apart from the comment in the YAML above there are also the following configurations that affect resources requirement configuration for generated Pods:

* Currently the section `SGInstanceProfile.spec.resources` is ignored unless the user sets any or all the fields `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.enableSet(Patroni|Cluster)(Cpu|Memory)Requests`. The idea is to deprecate all those fields and make the section always enabled so we can always have separated values for limits and requests (even if the user do not specify them directly).
* Setting to `true` field `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disablePatroniResourceRequirements` patroni contianer will not get any resources limits and requests (#2505 would allow to achieve the same result by setting `SGInstanceProfile.spec.cpu`, `SGInstanceProfile.spec.memory`, `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.cpu` and `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.memory` to `null`).
* Setting to `true` field `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disableClusterResourceRequirements` contianers that are not patroni will not get any resources limits and requests (#2505 would allow to achieve the same result by setting `SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.cpu` and `SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.memory` to `null`).

Indeed, I was able to reproduce the ~Bug locally. The behavior is cause by some buggy code fixed in [this change](https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/commit/9a8288de7ded255128fcda3732ea8c5f9528ec73#e49114eeaac3a130ffa104056b3c020bd20b6324_91_91) (also mentioned above) that makes the operator overwrite the `.status.os` and `.status.arch` fields and in [this change](https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/commit/ea416ea36888c17ac440db53682fe014cd083610#c27cac5696248d3f19d1d1432238e5ec1bf65f15_107_107) (both available in ~"target_version::1.3.0-beta1").

The wrong behavior is then that, when the operator overwrite the `.status.arch` and `.status.os` fields, the controller is not able to write then to the status since it does not fire the update until any extension or the patroni configuration is changed.

To fix the behavior we have to set the `.status.arch` to `x86_64` (or `aarch4` if you are running on ARM64) and `.status.os` to `linux`. To do so run the following commands:

```
kubectl get sgcluster -n "$CLUSTER_NAMESPACE" "$CLUSTER_NAME" -o json > "/tmp/sgcluster-$CLUSTER_NAEMSPACE-$CLUSTER_NAME.yaml"

# If you do not have `jq` you may just copy "/tmp/sgcluster-$CLUSTER_NAEMSPACE-$CLUSTER_NAME.yaml" to "/tmp/sgcluster-$CLUSTER_NAEMSPACE-$CLUSTER_NAME-with-arch-and-os.yaml" and add the fields manually
jq '.status.arch = "x86_64" | .status.os = "linux"' "/tmp/sgcluster-$CLUSTER_NAEMSPACE-$CLUSTER_NAME.yaml" > "/tmp/sgcluster-$CLUSTER_NAEMSPACE-$CLUSTER_NAME-with-arch-and-os.yaml"

kubectl replace --raw "/apis/stackgres.io/v1/namespaces/$CLUSTER_NAMESPACE/sgclusters/$CLUSTER_NAME/status" -f "/tmp/sgcluster-$CLUSTER_NAEMSPACE-$CLUSTER_NAME-with-arch-and-os.yaml"
```

## CPU

For CPU `cpuQuota` and `cpuPeriod` with cgroup v1 such field values [can be retrieved from `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us` and `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us` files](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-bwc.html#management). Issue:
Cluster pod is marked unavailable if any sidecar fails
If, for any reason, any sidecar container main process fails the container itself will stop being marked as ready. Consequently, the services that are backed by such container will be removed from the serivce's endpoints making them unreachable. This is OK for patroni, pgbouncer and envoy containers that participate actively in the service connection. For prometheus-postgres-exporter, fluent-bit, fluentd and postgres-util sidecars a service disruption have to be avoided if those processes crash. And, in such situation, the processes should be restarted anyway in a best effort fashion.

We already implemented [a script that wraps the main process and detect if they have to start it again in a loop](https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/blob/development/stackgres-k8s/src/operator/src/main/java/io/stackgres/operator/sidecars/fluentbit/FluentBit.java#L75) (like Kubernetes would do) without interfering with the readiness state of the whole Pod. Though, we are missing any means to inform the user of such failures (k8s events and sgcluster pod status). This solution just mitigate the problem since a crash in the script wrapper could trigger a service disruption too.

Seems that Kubernetes have an option that could allow to solve this problem using [Readiness Gates](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-readiness-gate). This feature allow to overwrite the readiness logic by introducing a custom pod condition that could be implemented with the local pod controller (see #331). The gate is available since k8s 1.12 and 1.11 in alpha so we could include this fix from %"StackGres 0.9". We could then monitor the status of readiness of container using status and updating our custom Pod condition.

Issue:
First iteration at a CRD for sharding: SGShardedCluster
I'd like to propose working on a new CRD, tentatively named `SGShardedCluster` to support automatic creation and management of sharded clusters in StackGres.

A sharded cluster is a set of clusters, which are architecturally independent of each other, but are logically linked by a given sharding technology that treats them and queries them, potentially, as a single, logical, single cluster. There is no in-core sharding solution, but several sharding technologies outside of Postgres core. Our aim is to potentially support several or all of them.

It is a non goal of this issue to develop a new sharding solution or solve problems or limitations of existing sharding solutions; but instead to leverage them and create a level of abstraction in the CRD that allows for very simple creation and management of sharded clusters.

Since the process of creating a generic CRD to support this use case is hard, and may require further iterations; it is a goal of this issue to discuss and implement a first, basic version of it.

Proposed guidelines for `SGShardedCluster`:
* The CRD should be marked as `alpha` for this issue and upcoming release, so we can iterate it freely.
* The CRD should not generate any resource-consumption resource in Kubernetes (e.g. `Pod`s) but rather delegate this to other Kubernetes or SG CRDs. Essentially, the job of the controller of this CRD is to generate other `SGCluster`s (and possibly `Secret`s, `Service`s, etc).
* The CRD should make room for more than one future sharding technology.
* For this first version, it is proposed that Citus is used for sharding.

[DISCUSSION]
[ahachete]: Here's my first proposal at how a very first version (simplified, a subset of what we will have) for the CRD:

```yaml
apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1alpha1
kind: SGShardedCluster
metadata:
  name: $string
spec:
  postgres:
    version: $string
  sharding: $sharding_enum
  coordinator:
    instances: $integer
    sgInstanceProfile: $string
    pods:
      persistentVolume:
        size: $string
  shards:
    clusters: $integer
    instancesPerCluster: $integer
    sgInstanceProfile: $string
    pods:
      persistentVolume:
        size: $string
  database: $string
  citus: $citus_object
  prometheusAutobind: $boolean

```

Notes:
* `.metadata.name` will be propagated as Patroni's [scope (cluster name)](https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/SETTINGS.html#global-universal)
* `.spec.database` is the database name that will be created and used across all nodes
* `$sharding_enum` will currently support only `citus` as a possible value
* `$citus_object` is for Citus-specific properties. Might be empty (not present). For now, I don't see we need anything here, but let's keep it part of the design. Obviously, it should be an error to have this field non-empty if `$sharding_enum` is not `citus`.
* `.spec.{coordinator,shards}` are not part of the `$citus_object` as they are quite technoogy-independent, and we should try to retrofit any future technology into them, if possible
* Maybe we can make `.spec.coordinator.pods.persistentVolume.size` have a default value of `1GiB`. In essence, these nodes do not need (almost) disk space, so we may setup a small default. Well, maybe they need some. Need to research particular cases for each technology.
* For the shards, I'd like to have the ability to "override" some of the "global settings for all shards" and allow to provide customized values per shard. Sometimes you want some specific shard to have more instances or a different instance profile. But let's keep it simple for now.
* Obvioulsy we lack a lot of other fields and subobjects here that could be copied verbatim from `SGCluster` and brought into the `coordinator` and/or `shards` fields. Let's keep it simple to get started and not propagate them for now.
* For Citus, we don't need to modify the SGPgConfig as Patroni will take care of adding the extension as the first parameter of `shared_preload_libraries`. But we will need to make it available, injecting it into the respective generated `SGCluster`s `.postgres.extensions[]` field.
* `.spec.prometheusAutobind`: this is copied from `SGCluster` but can we rename it to something more user-friendly like "enableObservability" or simply "observability"??
* It would be desirable that a single password is generated and written to a secret for the superuser password, and used for all the nodes.
* We need to discuss about the services being exposed, but for now I believe it's reasonable that we expose them with `SGCluster`'s defaults.
* We need to make sure all inter-node communication is allowed (networking, HBA, etc) and works.
* Anything not explicitly mentioned yet can be deferred to a later stage.

Issue:
OIDC Authentication does not work with SSL-terminating Proxy
### Summary

OIDC configuration is currently incompatible with SSL-terminating proxies such as ingress-nginx et al.

### Current Behaviour 

When deploying stackgres via Helm Chart with `enableHTTP` and configuring OIDC as authentication mechanism (AzureAD in this case),
the callback URL presented to the OIDC-Provider is presented as `http` instead of `https`.

#### Steps to reproduce

Deploy rest-api usind OIDC Authentication and expose HTTP endpoint for the service, e.g. setting  `enableHTTP: true` in the Helm chart values.
Add an ingress:

```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: stackgres
  namespace: db
spec:
  ingressClassName: private
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - stackgres.example.com
      secretName: stackgres-tls
  rules:
    - host: stackgres.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: stackgres-restapi
                port:
                  name: http
```

The callback URL presented to the provider is `http://stackgres.example.com/stackgres/auth/external`.

### Expected Behaviour

OIDC should present a HTTPS URL to the provider, e.g. `https://stackgres.example.com/stackgres/auth/external`

### Possible Solution

Enable more configuration options for configuring quarkus OIDC, especially `quarkus.oidc.authentication.force-redirect-https-scheme`.
One possibility for the Helm chart would be to set this property to `true` when `enableHTTP: true` is configured for the Service.

See https://quarkus.io/guides/security-openid-connect-web-authentication#running-behind-a-reverse-proxy

The proxy and header configuration mentioned in the documentation was not required in the case of the k8s ingress-nginx as proxy.

An additional/alternative escape hatch, for the Helm chart at least, would be the possibility to define additional
custom volumes/mounts and/or adding one ore more generic ConfigMaps/Secrets as env variable sources.

### Environment

- StackGres version: Helm Chart version 1.4.0
- Kubernetes version: 1.21.14
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: HEtzner cloud

[xaviersierra]: Unfortunately we can’t fix this issue until EKS fix [its CSR certificate issue](https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/tree/main-1.1/stackgres-k8s/src/operator/src/main/resources). 

In the meantime we can’t avoid this situation by manually creating the certificates. 

This can be done using cert-manager. Here are some instructions it can be done assuming that we want to install StackGres in a namespace named stackgres: 

1. Install cert-manager.  

cert-manager can be installed by running the following command:
``` sh
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.8.0/cert-manager.yaml
```

2. Configure a self signed certificate Issuer applying the following yaml.

``` yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Issuer
metadata:
  name: stackgres-self-issuer
  namespace: stackgres
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
```

3. Create a self signed certificate, it will be used by the CA to sign certificates. This can be done by applying the following yaml:

``` yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: stackgres-ca
  namespace: stackgres
spec:
  isCA: true
  commonName: stackgres-ca
  secretName: root-secret
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
  issuerRef:
    name: stackgres-self-issuer
    kind: Issuer
    group: cert-manager.io
```

4. Create a CA issuer.

``` yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Issuer
metadata:
  name: stackgres-ca-issuer
  namespace: stackgres
spec:
  ca:
    secretName: root-secret
```

5. Create the operator certificate. Notice the DNS names, they are required in order for StackGres to work. 
 
``` yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: stckgres-operator-cert
  namespace: stackgres
spec:
  secretName: stackgres-operator-tls
  duration: 2160h
  renewBefore: 360h
  subject:
    organizations:
      - Ongres
  isCA: false
  privateKey:
    algorithm: RSA
    encoding: PKCS1
    size: 2048
  usages:
    - server auth
    - client auth
  dnsNames:
    - stackgres-operator
    - stackgres-operator.stackgres
    - stackgres-operator.stackgres.svc
    - stackgres-operator.stackgres.svc.cluster.local
  issuerRef:
    name: stackgres-ca-issuer
    kind: Issuer
    group: cert-manager.io
```

The above yaml will produce a secret named stackgres-operator-tls in the stackgres namespace, that holds the private and public keys. 

Now we can install stackgres with the following script:

``` sh
CERT_KEY=$(kubectl get secrets -n stackgres stackgres-operator-tls -o json | jq '.data["tls.key"]' -r)
CERT_CRT=$(kubectl get secrets -n stackgres stackgres-operator-tls -o json | jq '.data["tls.crt"]' -r)

helm install --namespace stackgres stackgres-operator \
  --set-string adminui.service.type=LoadBalancer \
  --version 1.1.0 \
  --set cert.key="$CERT_KEY" \
  --set cert.crt="$CERT_CRT" \
  stackgres-charts/stackgres-operator
```

Setting the cert.key and cert.crt would prevent StackGres from using CSR. Notice that the release name and release namespace matches the DNS certificates.

Issue:
Develop pod-local StackGres Controller
Currently, StackGres works as an operator, that runs as a separate pod (from the Postgres cluster pods). From there, it interacts with the Kubernetes API to perform StackGres actions, including creating and destroying pods and many other actions.

However, it doesn't have a clear way to interact with the clusters once created. In particular, it has no way to explicitly run commands / take some actions inside of some of the containers of the StackGres pods. And some maintenance operations (like for example reloading configuration files) require to run some commands on those containers.

Rather than creating custom scripts, or executing commands with the Kubernetes API, the team has decided to continue leveraging the _sidecar pattern_ and implement this via a sidecar container that will act as a pod-local StackGres controller.

This controller will expose an HTTP API that the "main/central" controller will be called. This would also help to abstract the implementation of how those actions are executed within the pod containers.

Similarly to other HTTP APIs used by StackGres, this HTTP API will follow [RFC-7807](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7807) for communicating back errors. This pod-local controller will be a separate container, where a Java-developed software compiled to native code via GraalVM will be running.

For a first implementation, this pod-local controller must implement the following operations. Also suggested implementation details are proposed as part of this issue:

* [ ]  ~~Reload Postgres configuration. Postgres configuration (both `postgresql.conf` and `pg_hba.conf`) is currently handled via Patroni. Patroni stores this configuration as a JSON within and Endpoint annotation --which is backed by K8s etcd--. Whenever it is changed, Patroni propagates these changes to all nodes of the cluster automatically. However, they are not refreshed. Implementation: ideally, Patroni's own HTTP API should be called. It exposes a `POST /reload` method that handles precisely this use case. It may also be an option to execute the command `patronictl reload`, but is less desirable.~~

* [ ]  Reload Pgbouncer configuration. PGbouncer provides a command to reload the configuration (see [RELOAD](http://www.pgbouncer.org/usage.html)) that will perform this task. This requires access to the administrative database of pgbouncer (typically called `pgbouncer`, but this depends on the configuration). Ideally, this may be over localhost using the Postgres protocol, but may happen otherwise. Another possible, although less desirable implementation, is to `kill -HUP` pgbouncer's process, getting the pid from the `pgbouncer.pid` or similar file.


One common issue to these methods is to ensure that the configuration change has been adequately propagated to the pod **before** the reload method is called. There may be a race condition here since propagation of changes via the downward API or annotations on objects is asynchronous with respect to the change operation. One way to avoid this problem is to introduce a version field as part of every configuration, that is monotonically increased whenever any change is performed. Then, the reload operations must also specify which version they are expecting the configuration to be at. The reload mechanism (executed by the pod-local controller) must check that the version of the configuration materialized on the filesystem matches the one requested via the web service; or wait with some retries until it gets updated. Return an error if after several retries that version got never updated.

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: I like the idea of a container that handles operations specific to a node in a StackGres cluster but I have some concerns about making it accessible through a REST API.

IMHO I see a better approach would be to make this pod-local component use the kubernetes REST API directly. In particular, using directly kubernetes REST API, by listen for changes in the sgcluster CR and take action based on the state of that resource. The state will then be updated by the pod-local component when the operation has been completed. This reduce the complexity of having a REST API, a client for that API and all the logic in the middle in order to manage sgcluster status in kubernetes REST API.

Apart from the mechanism to actually reload a configuration I would like to give context (and some corrections) on the mechanism to know a configuration has been updated on disk with the required version prior executing the reload or has been updated to the required version (in case the former option is not available):

* In the case of pgbouncer it could be done by adding the sgconnectionpoolingconfig resource version and a md5 hash of config file content and resource version value (both mounted as files). Resource version allow to check the version is the same as the mounted one. The md5 hash allow to check that the mount of files is not in a transitory state (i.e. configuration is consistent with the version).
* In the case of patroni/postgresql, since patroni updates the version with his own mechanism reading it from a kubernetes entpoints's annotation (updated by the operator), it is most probably updated using always the correct configuration (thanks to consistence of resources enforced by etcd).

This could be a possible implementation of the status part in sgcluster CR to reload configuration for postgresql and pgbouncer:

```
apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: StackGresCluster
metadata:
  name: test
...
status:
  ...
  pgConfigVersion: <sgpgconfig resource version>
  connectionPoolingConfigVersion: <sgconnectionpoolingconfig resource version>
  pods:
    - name: test-0
      conditions:
        - type: PatroniRequiresReload
          status: (true|false)
        - type: PgBouncerRequiresReload
          status: (true|false)
          
```

[ahachete]: I agree with this approach @teoincontatto. It's a very good idea. [Kubernetes documentation define the `status` subresource as](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/):

>  Allows fine-grained access control where user writes the spec section and the controller writes the status section.

so it makes sense to have this section for "controller-communication". The fact that is not controller->user and rather controller->{local controller, user} is irrelevant from this perspective.

Now, what I would encode into this field, instead of the proposed data structure above, is more of a "pending operations queue". Once operations are dequeued and properly executed, they are logged as an `Event`, and removed from the Status pending operations. Something like:

```
apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: StackGresCluster
metadata:
  name: test
...
status:
  ...
  pendingOperations:
    - type: ReloadPostgresConfiguration
      pod: test-0
      configRevision: $sgpgconfig_revision
    - ...
```

Obviously, a reload operation on a whole cluster may require several operations queued (one per pod), but that's fine and similar to the model proposed above.

[teoincontatto]: After reviewing naming we should call the "revision" as "resource version" to be sure we are talking of the correct thing, sorry for the mistake I initially introduced (I updated my previous comment to reflect this statement).

I am ok (mostly) with using a operation queue. It reminds me of some approach used in another project :wink:. But to truly accept it I would like to mention some concerns that cross my mind:

* Conditions are easy to query in case we want a simple response yes/no on a fact: is latest configuration used?

* Operations will always follow the order specified by the queue independently of the actual state of the components running inside the pods or the state of kubernetes resources.

It is true that using conditions only the last operation of a type would be performed and we lose sequence here, but for the case of configuration reload you just need the last configuration to be reloaded.

* I wonder the queue could grow without limit.

We could mitigate that by cleaning duplicated operation but that would not solve the growth problem completely. If we use the conditions method it eliminates completely the growth problem.

* Conditions are more standard in kubernetes and user will be more used to them.

[ahachete]: I agree with "resource version".

I don't mind going for conditions, I think they will as of now do the job. But I still see them more limited. They represent a final state, rather than a sequences of state changes, which the operations queue will hold. For example, if two reload operations are sent, and you want to understand the result (success or fail) independently, you would not be able to.

Now, if we'd go for the operations queue, and addressing your very valid concerns, I'd say:
*  Add an UUID to every operation. This will be necessary to identify this in the Events log.
*  Add also an expiration timestamp to every operation. The pod-local controller will be able to remove from the queue any expired operation without running it (but logging it as an Event that was expired).
*  Allow out-of-order polling from the queue --if that would be needed.

[ahachete]: I'd also like to comment on the revisions for the configuration. Splitting into a separate subthread.

On the connection pooling side, it is clear that we can compute a hash and pass that. We just need to make sure we properly take into account non-present values (default values).

On the Patroni/Postgres side: we still need a versioning or hashing mechanism, as it is not enough that Patroni distributes the configuration automatically. It does, but we don't know if, at the time the "reload postgres" operation is queued, the changes to the configuration have been materialized yet on the pod. They will be consistent in etcd, as you say, but they are AFAIK asynchronously (i.e. eventually consistent) propagated via Downward API. So we can't just assume changes will be local to the pod once the enqueued reload operation arrives via the CRD.

[teoincontatto]: Actually in the case of Patroni/Postgres it is not using downward API. Patroni reads his endpoints's annotation, render the configuration and write it on disk. IMHO the problem is to know when the configuration has been updated and reloaded.

I searched through the code and I found that the patroni API do not wait for the configuration to take effect:

```
...
    @check_auth
    def do_POST_reload(self):
        self.server.patroni.sighup_handler()
        self._write_response(202, 'reload scheduled')

...
```

The `sighup_handler()` function set a flag that is later checked in a loop.

Seems that the only way to be sure a configuration has been correctly updated and reloaded is with a [postgresql custom option](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/12/runtime-config-custom.html). Let's call it `stackgres.sgpgconfig_resource_version`.

[ahachete]: If this is the case, then I agree on using the custom configuration option.

[ahachete]: I got "privileged" information from Patroni devs ;)

> Regarding configuration change: REST API acts only as a proxy, i.e. updates the endpoint annotations and nothing more.
> All Patroni instances are asynchronously watching for changes of the endpoint and in case if the configuration doesn't match it will try to apply it (generate postgresql.conf and send sighup to postgres)
> There is no need to call `/reload endpoint`. It is useful only in two cases:
> 1. you changed patroni.yaml and want to apply these changes
> 1. you manage parts of postgres configuration by external tools and want to reload postgres.

[teoincontatto]: Nice to know! :)

This mean we still have to go by the custom option though

[ahachete]: As I understand it, we don't need any custom parameter. We don't actually need to do anything. As soon as Patroni will see a change in the configuration, it will update `postgresql.conf` and SIGHUP Postgres. In other words, there's nothing else we need to do. The pod-local controller should only worry, for now, about reloading pgbouncer.

```yaml
apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1
kind: SGInstanceProfile
spec:
  hugePages:
    hugepages-2Mi: <N>(Mi|Gi|Ti) # The amount of huge pages of size 2Mi to assign to the Patroni container

- Huge Pages affect shared_buffers only as found in [Postgres Docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/kernel-resources.html#LINUX-HUGE-PAGES):

> Using huge pages reduces overhead when using large contiguous chunks of memory, as PostgreSQL does, particularly when using large values of shared_buffers. 

Meaning that we should round up the shared_buffers to the next page size available (4k, **2M**, 1G -- used mostly for kernel optimizations). We can set it as a default to enable HP on `shared_buffers` above 2GB, and round the requested amount of pages to `shared buffers in MB`/2MB. 

- huge_pages on `try` may lead to THP usage which is not desirable and not available to tweak in K8s without root privileges.

[ahachete]: > We can set it as a default to enable HP on `shared_buffers` above 2GB

apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1

spec:
...

[ahachete]: Reopen to leave some thought as this is probably the most appropriate place. Feel free @xaviersierra to ACK and add this, keeping this re-opened; close and dismiss; or open a new issue related to this one if that would be better.

Basically, one of the goals of this new CRD is to allow other uses of object storage that are not backups. Potentially we can use tools within StackGres that would read and/or write to that object storage that, again, are not backups.

Shouldn't we, then, use some relative path (on top of any path that the user may have configured within the object storage) to separate the storage of our own subystems? We could even use the reverse DNS name of the CRD responsible for that storage. E.g.:

`${bucket}/${user_path}/io.stackgres.sgbackup/...`      # current backups

`${bucket}/${user_path}/io.stackgres.sgdbops/...`       # for example a pg_dump (see #990)

WDYT?

[teoincontatto]: The proposed feature is related to [this comment](https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/issues/1383#note_709021369). The big problem here is that `SGBackup` will still use a copy of the `SGObjectStorage` so that we need to provide a backward compatible mechanism to point an existing `SGBackup` to the current implementation of the path (`${bucket}/${user_path}/${cluster_namespace}/${cluster_name}`). The proposed solution in the comment above to add a `finalPath` field that is able to override completely the composed value so that old `SGBackup`s (and `SGBackupConfig`s) points to the old path have to be applied to the `SGObjectStorage` too (that is actually inlined in `SGBackup`).

A good side effect of having a `finalPath` is that an `SGObjectStorage` could point to custom user location. And that is a requirement, for example, in order to be able to restore a backup or a pg_dump generated outside of StackGres or to be used by [WAL-based SGCluster replication](#866).

In any case this should be addressed in a separate issue and close this one that has been already merged.

Issue:
Allow SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.xxx.memory to be optional
### Problem to solve

I have a cluster running with this instance profile:

```yaml
apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1
kind: SGInstanceProfile
metadata:
  name: acme
spec:
  cpu: "4"
  memory: "16Gi"
```

the 4000m/16Gi request goes to patroni and the other containers such as envoy and pgbouncer are automatically assigned derived requests. I end up with pods that request 6000m cpu, which I am not pleased with.

I would like to be able to limit cpu usage for the non-patroni pods (better yet, setup requests and limits separately, though this is a different story). `SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.envoy.cpu` does exactly that, but it requires me to fill in `.memory` as well. As an operator, I don't want to setup memory requests. I am not aware of peculiarities of particular services and I would be very happy with the defaults.

### Proposal

`SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.xxx.memory` should be optional. If not provided by an operator, the defaults should be used (same defaults that are used if `SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers` is not provided at all).

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: This is an interesting case. Current implementation is as follow.

For patroni container:

* `SGInstanceProfile.spec.cpu` and `SGInstanceProfile.spec.memory` are both required and they set both limits and requests for CPU and memory of the patroni container. To override the requests see below. You can ignore both limits and requests by setting `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disablePatroniResourceRequirements` to `true`.
* `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.cpu` is optional and allows to override the requests for the CPU of patroni container. You can enable this section by setting `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.enableSetPatroniCpuRequests` to `true`.
* `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.memory` is optional and allows to override the requests for the memory of patroni container. You can enable this section by setting `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.enableSetPatroniMemoryRequests` to `true`.

For any other container (or init containers, just replace `containers` with `initContainers` in the field paths):

* `SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.*.cpu` and `SGInstanceProfile.spec.containers.*.memory` are both required and they set both limits and requests for CPU and memory of a container (except patroni, see above). To override the requests see below. You can ignore both limits and requests by setting `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.disableClusterResourceRequirements` to `true`.
* `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.containers.*.cpu` is optional and allows to override the requests for the CPU of a container (except patroni, see above). You can enable this section by setting `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.enableSetClusterCpuRequests` to `true`.
* `SGInstanceProfile.spec.requests.containers.*.memory` is optional and allows to override the requests for the memory of a container (except patroni, see above). You can enable this section by setting `SGCluster.spec.nonProductionOptions.enableSetClusterMemoryRequests` to `true`.

[teoincontatto]: So, you may not avoid setting limits but, at least, you can set it to a high value and requests to a lower one. We may consider allow to disable just limits so I leave this issue as a ~"Feature Request"

[ahachete]: While I agree that we cannot support a release that we cannot even test, I'd try to be here as lenient as possible. As long as we don't require changes in the APIs that we use/expose that won't work on these versions, why not leave it more as an "untested" rather than blocking its installation?

Some users are (unfortunately) using old Kubernetes versions.

[jorsol]: Users that are (unfortunately) using older Kubernetes versions are probably using an older StackGres release.

We could leave it as an "untested" (or more clearly "unsupported") option, but IMHO that could cause more harm than good, but the point here is that Kubernetes is moving fast, and trying to support many older versions does not make sense (unless there are explicit customers that ask for it).

And even if the APIs don't require changes, the testing should at least target a supported version (right now it target 1.16).

[ahachete]: Yes, I agree is not ideal and we definitely should clearly advertise what versions of K8s are properly tested and validated.

But having said that, if we can keep as wide as possible the versions that a) we test; and b) that we still publish as "unsupported", the better, since we give chances to users that may be tied to older versions.

And then we introduce strict limits when we rely on features that are not available on older K8s versions (e.g. as of now, `1.15` or below won't be reasonable).

[teoincontatto]: Seems that some old Kubernetes versions (at least 1.16) are affected by a bug for the Server Side Apply. When doing SSA to an existing resource, by removing an existing field that represent a section (a JSON object) that is present in the `.metadata.managedFields` section only for the same `fieldManager` that perform the SSA, the field is not removed from the resource, only from the `.metadata.managedFields` section. Issue:
Add backupPath to SGCluster, SGBackup and SGDbOps (for op majorVersionUpgrade)
The path of the storage for backups are limited to a predefined path. We have to address the following problems:

1. Issue #1383 and functionality suggested in [this comment](https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/issues/1564#note_832735008) requires to modify the internal composition of the final path used to store backups or to be able to store other objects like SQL dumps.
2. Issue #1589 requires to be able to point to a custom path of a storage in order to read WAL-files provided by a cluster working in an external Kubernetes cluster or event one that is not necessarily a StackGres cluster.
3. Issue #200 requires to point to a custom path of a storage in order to read backups that were not necessarily being produced by a StackGres cluster.

## Implementation plan

A new `backupPath` field for the backup path in the storage under following sections:

* `.spec.configurations.backupPath` in `SGCluster` 
* `.status.backupPath` in `SGBackup`

The `backupPath` field will allow an user to overwrite (if specified) any path composed internally for store/read backups and WAL files with wal-g. Also, to accommodate #1383 and https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/issues/1564#note_832735008 the default `backupPath` to read/write backups will be generated as:

`"sgbackups.stackgres.io/${cluster_namespace}/${cluster_name}/${postgres_major_version}"`

Previous version of `SGCluster` and `SGBackup` will generate a `backupPath` field with the value constructed using the current implementation:

`"${path:-}/${cluster_namespace}/${cluster_name}"`

Additionally, following fields will be deprecated by forbidding his usage for new CR created:

* `.spec.[s3|compatibleS3|gcs|azureBlob].path` in `SGObjectStorage`
* `.spec.storage.[s3|compatibleS3|gcs|azureBlob].path` in `SGBackupConfig`

## Acceptance Criteria

Addition of `backupPath` field must allow backward compatibility with previous version of StackGres.

Documentation of `backupPath` field must indicate the use cases where an user may want to set it. For example use cases like #200 or #1589.

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: I wonder if adding a `finalPath` on `SGObjectStorage` is maybe the wrong thing to do since an `SGObjectStorage` will be referenced by multiple kind of custom resources:

* `SGCluster` for the backups and WAL shipping (see #866)
* `SGBackup` in order to restore a backup
* `SGDbOps` in order to create an SQL dump (see #990)

Having a `finalPath` in a referenced resource may screw things up easily if a user do not realize he/she have to copy the `SGObjectStorage` that is used more than once to change the `path` or the `finalPath`.

IMO we should instead put this `finalPath` field together with were references of `SGObjectStorage` goes so that the reference is no longer the name of the `SGObjectStorage` alone but a combination of `name` and `path`. Just like for `ConfigMap` and `Secret` where you reference a key of the resource. So you will reference a path of the `SGObjectStorage` resource. We may also make the path something that is set by default to some location (e.g. `sgbackups.stackgres.io/${cluster_namespace}/${cluster_name}/${postgres_major_version}` for a backup). Let's call all those sections that reference a path of an `SGObjectStorage` with the name `sgObjectStoragePathSelector` with the following proposed model:

```yaml
sgObjectStoragePathSelector:
  name: <string> # The name of an `SGObjectStorage`
  path: <string> # The path that will be used in the object storage. Default to `...`.
```

We can then deprecate the field `.spec.storage.[s3|compatibleS3|gcs|azureBlob].path` in `SGBackupConfig` since the user may change the `path` in the reference that will be always the final path to whatever he/she wants.

This will require to bump the `apiVersion` of `SGCluster` and `SGBackup` to `v1.1` but I think is a better approach since it will allow to truly reuse a single `SGObjectStorage` for multiple purpose.

WDYT?

Also, this affect section `.spec.configurations.backups` implemented by #862 that will require to add a new field that will replace the `backupPath` field. A proposition for the name is simply `.spec.configurations.backups[].path` since under section `.spec.configurations.backups` it is clear that we refer to a path of a backup. In any case this will be implemented in a separate issue since #862 is still not merged to main branch.

Issue:
Labels are too generic and should be changed to avoid collisions
### Problem to solve

Many labels generated by StackGres are too generic and they should be changed in order to avoid collisions.

### Further details

A particular case where labels are too generic are the `cluster` and `disruptable` labels that are set with a value of `true` or `false`. It is may occur that StackGres labels collide with user labels. In general this is not true for the `app` label that is enough well known in order to avoid such situation since the value of such label is much more meaningful.

### Proposal

We should prefix all the StackGres labels excluding the `app` label with the `stackgres.io/` prefix.

### Testing

We should make sure that after upgrading the cluster the secutiry upgrade takes care of such change gracefully and the upgrade do not end in a failing cluster.

## Acceptance Criteria

All labels (except `app`) are all prefixed with `stackgres.io/` and secutiry upgrade is capable of handle gracefully the transition from the old set of labels.

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: For an already existing cluster, prefixing the labels with `stackgres.io/` of the generated resources and of the Pods and PersistentVolumeClaims of the cluster's StatefulSet, we end up with Patroni in an unstable state. The labels used to find pods of the cluster are initially unchanged and, since Pods maintain previous labels, same pods are found. But after adding or re-creating a Pod, it spin up without the old set of labels so that Patroni in the old Pods do not see those new or re-created Pods. This breaks completely Patroni and also the restart operation that is not able to perform the switchover and has no more a reliable way of detecting the cluster members since it rely on the Patroni REST API that is served by any instance of Patroni from any Pod in the cluster.

Even if, after an heavy refactor of the code, we are able to apply this change only after a security upgrade operation we should also change the operation in order to reduce the size of the cluster to 1, perform the version upgrade, restart the single remaining instance and then scale back the cluster to the previous size. This to avoid performing the switchover that this change breaks but it also introduce a longer disruption window. But due to the side effect of the change it seems not possible to prevent a longer disruption window in any scenario.

Another option, that might be the sweet point that would lower the complexity of the change and avoid any pitfall, would be to make the labels prefix to appear in the field `.status.labelPrefix` of an `SGCluster`. By default it would be `stackgres.io/` and set an empty one on any cluster with a previous version of StackGres.

[teoincontatto]: Finally a slightly different approach has been implemented by allowing the `.status.labelPrefix` field to be null and defaulting its value to `stackgres.io/`. This way new clusters will not be polluted with such value.

[jorsol]: This issue reminds me about issue https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/-/issues/343, right now `app` is not affected here, yet we might consider to use the prefix `app.kubernetes.io` for some metadata labels, like `app`.

[teoincontatto]: I agree, but I would not block this issue to include such change since !1100 is already ~"workflow::In Review". Anyway we may schedule #343 for the next release ~"target_version::1.3.0".

[jorsol]: Sure, it's not a blocker at all, just mention it to not forget about it.

Issue:
Implement a correct solution for resources of cluster's pods
Currently the cluster is created setting uniquely resources request and limit on the patroni container but a correct solution would be to split the resources limit and request among all containers of the cluster's pods. We should research the correct solution to this problem making sure that:

* Pod total resources limit and request are shared among all containers and the sum of resources limit and request is equals to the one specified in the profile.
* Pod resources limit and request should be balanced in a way that respect the role of each container. We should make sure each container has the right amount of memory and cpu for it to operate correctly and at best performance possible with that profile configuration.
* Resources limit and request are correctly specified in the configuration of a profile. Currently we set a value for cpu and memory and use that in both resource limit and request, we should check this is a correct approach.

# Proposal

This is a proposal to enhance `SGInstanceProfile`  in order to set the resource requirements for containers and init containers and a similar section to include with #820 or implement with this issue if #820 get implemented before this one:

```yaml
apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1
kind: SGInstanceProfile
spec:
  cpu: 16000
  memory: 64Gi
  containers:
    pgbouncer:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 64Mi
    envoy:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 64Mi
    prometheus-postgres-exporter:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    postgres-util:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    fluent-bit:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    fluentd:
      cpu: 4000
      memory: 2Gi
    cluster-controller: # Could be applied also to distributedlogs-controller
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 512Mi # Fix #1566 to improve this
  initContainers:
    setup-arbitrary-user:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    setup-data-paths:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    relocate-binaries:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    setup-scripts:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    pgbouncer-auth-file:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
    cluster-reconciliation-cycle: # Could be applied also to distributedlogs-reconciliation-cycle
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 512Mi # Fix #1566 to improve this
    major-version-upgrade:
      cpu: 16000
      memory: 64Gi
    reset-patroni:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 8Mi
```

If the user do not specify a container sub-section in the `.spec.containers` or `.spec.initContainers` section here are the proposed formulas to calculate the values of such sub-sections on creation of `sGInstanceProfile`:

> Those values may be lowered. Also in those cases the requests may be lower than the limit when it comes to apply this resource requirements to specified containers in order to use the shared CPUs when [CPU manager policy is set to static](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/cpu-management-policies/#static-policy) in order to be in the `Burstable` group and use the shared pool of CPUs. 

* For `pgbouncer`:

  * `cpu` as millicpu: `min(1000, floor(toMillicpu(".spec.cpu") / 16))` 
  * `memory` as Mi: `64`

With `64Mi` PgBouncer should be able to handle 4096 connections. See https://www.pgbouncer.org/features.html

> Low memory requirements (2 kB per connection by default). This is because PgBouncer does not need to see full packets at once.

* For `envoy`:

[teoincontatto]: There are two conditions in order to take advantage of the `Guaranteed` containers that run on exclusive CPUs:

* `kubelet` must have the parameter `--cpu-manager-policy` set to `strict`
* Container must have the `.resources.limit.cpu` equals to `.resources.requests.cpu` and the value must be an integer (i.e. not a fraction).

[teoincontatto]: Considering what we currently have:

* `sginstanceprofile` define both request and limit for CPU and memory as a single value for each or separately (when #820 will be implemented). We should consider those values as global for each cluster Pod.
* A Pod of a `sgcluster` or `sgdistributedlogs` can create a set of containers. Those are patroni, pgbouncer, envoy, prometheus-postgres-exporter, postgres-util, fluent-bit and fluentd. The goal is to set resources request and limit for each container by sharing the request defined in the `sginstanceprofile`.
* Stats from cluster's pods should be fine grained at level of container (when #823 will be implemented). 

IMO we should follow these steps in order to have a first glace of the strategy to follow:

* Init containers can use all the resources defined in `sginstanceprofile` since they run sequentially.
* Gather statistic of a running environment for each container of the cluster's Pod.
* Find out, using gathered stats, the maximum resources required for each container in order to set it as the request and limit base for such container except patroni that will have request and limit set to the value defined in `sginstanceprofile` minus the sum of the reuqest and limit that have been set to for other containers. 
* Extend `sginstanceprofile` in order to allow the user to overwrite resource request and limit for each container except patroni. A field `.spec.containers` containing a map of `<container name>` and an object with fields `memory` and `cpu` that will be filled by default with values from previous step.

Here is an example of how `sginstanceprofile` will look like (should be modified when #820 will be implemented):

```yaml
apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1
kind: SGInstanceProfile
spec:
  cpu: 16000
  memory: 64Gi
  containers:
    pgbouncer:
      cpu: 1000
      memory: 64Mi
    envoy:
      cpu: 4000
      memory: 16Mi
    prometheus-postgres-exporter:
      cpu: 250
      memory: 8Mi
    postgres-util:
      cpu: 250
      memory: 8Mi
    fluent-bit:
      cpu: 250
      memory: 8Mi
    fluentd:
      cpu: 4000
      memory: 32Mi
```

In this example the resources request and limit set for patroni in an `sgcluster` with all containers (patroni, pgbouncer, envoy, prometheus-postgres-exporter, postgres-util and fluent-bit) would be:

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
   - name: patroni
     resources:
       limits:
         cpu: 10250
         memory: 65432Mi
       requests:
         cpu: 10250
         memory: 65432Mi
```

[teoincontatto]: If it was not clear from the description above the `.spec.containers` field of `sginstanceprofile` is filled automatically by a mutating webhook using values we collected from stats if the user does not specify it.

Issue:
Enhance Web Console's usability/discoverability of the "enable monitoring" option when creating a cluster
Monitoring is one of the most important features you may want from a Postgres cluster. In SG it is not enabled by default, and that's probably fine. It also depends on the user installing the optional dependencies that the user requires for monitoring, and we don't have much control over that.

However, if you have installed the dependencies, discovering how to enable monitoring for the cluster is not immediate. It is "hidden" under `Advanced options` and then `Sidecars`. Not very intuitive.

It actually makes sense where it is, since it requires deploying a sidecar. However, we should *also* make it more accessible. Therefore I propose to add in the main screen, `Cluster` section, at the bottom, a simple checkbox with the following text and tooltip:

* Text: _Enable monitoring_
* Tooltip: _StackGres supports enabling automatic monitoring for your Postgres cluster, but you need to provide or install the [Prometheus stack as a pre-requisite](https://stackgres.io/doc/latest/install/prerequisites/monitoring/). Then, check this option to configure automatically sending metrics to the Prometheus stack_.

This won't change anything under the `Sidecars` section, other than the enabled/disabled status in both the `Cluster` and `Sidecars` section needs to stay in sync.

Issue:
Refactor Backups Jobs handling
### Problem to solve

If SGBackup requires a longer than the scheduled interval between backups, the backup jobs start to stack up waiting for the job lock to be released.

### Further details

Given a backup scheduling that is too short for a SGBackup to complete, the k8s CronJob will keep launching new jobs. 

In this situation, a new SGbackup will not run until the job lock is released, nonetheless the job pod is created and reserving memory and cpu resources. Also it regularly looks it 

If the situation continues, the SGBackups could saturate the cpu and memory resources of the k8s cluster, besides, it will frequently call the k8s api to check if lock has been released. 

To illustrate this scenario. Let's say that a backup schedule is "*/1 * * * *", which means that full backup will be executed every minute, and also, a full backup requires 90 seconds to complete. 

At the minute 3 we would have:
- 1 backup completed
- 1 backup running
- 1 backup waiting for the lock to be released

At minute 10, we would have:
- 6 backups completed
- 1 backup running
- 2 backups waiting for the lock to be released

As the situation continues, there will be more and more SGBackups waiting to be executed. 

This scenario has another drawback, it affects how DbObs jobs are performed. 

DbOps Jobs tries to acquire the SGCluster lock the same way that SGBackup does. Therefore if many jobs (Backups or DbOps) are waiting for the lock to be released, then they would all compete to acquire the lock first, which means that a regular DbOps would have to wait a long time before it is executed. 

Backup Jobs has another problem, which is the backup reconciliation. 

The backup reconciliation process is performed just after the backup has been completed, in the same job of the backup. 

This dependency has the inconvenient that if the backup process fails, then the backup reconciliation is not performed. 

### Proposal

There are several alternatives that can be implemented to address this problem. 

1. The simplest solution is to make the backup job to check if there is an already running backup, if there is any, it terminates itself. Ideally, generating an event informing that a backup schedule was missing. 

This approach has the advantage that it should be fast to implement, nonetheless it doesn't decople the backup reconciliation from the backup job and it could still interfere with DbOps jobs. Therefore it could be considered as a first step but not as a full solution. 

2. Move backup logic into the cluster-controller. 

There is already an issue for this. The main advantages here are:
- It should perform faster than a shell script implementation. 
- Less interactions between pods and the k8s API are required. 
- It would allow us to make the backups more resilient to network issues. 
- It could give us more decoupling between the backup process and the backup reconciliation. 
- It would allow us to not rely on the k8s CronJobs, and use something like Quartz. And would that give more scheduling options than what k8s provides. 

Also it has it downsides:
- Adding a library like Quartz will increase the size of the cluster-controller image, and we could have to deal with native image generation issues.
- It would have more memory footprint, making SGCluster nodes heavier. 
- It doesn’t solve the interference with the DbOps. 
- it would need to have a sort of consensus algorithm in order to ensure that only the leader performs the backup. 

3. Create a jobs controller pod. 
This controller would be a container that runs in a separate pod of a SGCluster. The main idea is that it should orchestrate all jobs that are related to a particular SGCluster. 

This would allow us to implement a priority queue between jobs that has conflicts in schedule. 

For instance if a DbOps restart is scheduled to be performed at the same time as the backup, it could decide to run the restart first and then backup. 

In order to not implement the backup logic inside jobs controller pod a REST API endpoint could be exposed by the cluster-controller, which when called, performs the backup. 

``` mermaid
graph TD
    O[StackGres Operator]
    subgraph SGCluster 1
      subgraph Leader Pod
        P1[Patroni]
        C1[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph Replica Pod
        RP1[Patroni]
        RC1[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph JP1 [Jobs Controller Pod]
        J1[JobsController] -- http --> C1
      end
    end
    O -- deploys --> J1
    subgraph SGCluster 2
      subgraph Leader Pod
        P2[Patroni]
        C2[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph Replica Pod
        RP2[Patroni]
        RC2[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph JP2 [Jobs Controller Pod]
          J2[JobsController] -- http --> C2
      end    
    end
    O -- deploys --> J2
```

The advantages of this approach are:
- It frees the operator from managing DbOps Jobs, reducing its complexity. 
- Since the scheduler runs on a single pod it doesn’t need a consensus verification. 
- It would reduce the interference between backups and DbOps
- It provides more decoupling between the backup process and the backup reconciliation

Nonetheless, it comes with a big disadvantage, it's significantly harder to code which would take more time. 

4. Create a storage-controller alongside the jobs-controller. 

This component would be a manager of a SGObjectStorage, and therefore handle the backup reconciliation. The main goal of this component is to make the backup reconciliation totally independent of a SGCluster. 

This component could also solve some of the current issues of the backup reconciliation, like the unintentional deletion of backups. 

Since the lifecycle of the storage-controller is not related tied to SGCluster, the backup reconciliation could still work even if the SGCluster its deleted.

``` mermaid
graph TD
    O[StackGres Operator]
    subgraph SGCluster 1
      subgraph Leader Pod
        P1[Patroni]
        C1[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph Replica Pod
        RP1[Patroni]
        RC1[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph JP1 [Jobs Controller Pod]
        J1[JobsController] -- http --> C1
      end
    end
    O -- deploys --> J1
    subgraph SGCluster 2
      subgraph Leader Pod
        P2[Patroni]
        C2[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph Replica Pod
        RP2[Patroni]
        RC2[ClusterController]
      end
      subgraph JP2 [Jobs Controller Pod]
          J2[JobsController] -- http --> C2
      end    
    end
    O -- deploys --> J2
    O -- deploys --> storage-controller
```

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: > # Further details
> ...
> DbOps Jobs tries to acquire the SGCluster lock the same way that SGBackup does. ...

A correction here: the backup Jobs do not lock on the `SGCluster` custom resource they do so on the `CronJob` resource that is associated to the `SGCluster`.

> # Proposal
> ...
> 2. Move backup logic into the cluster-controller.
> ...
> it would need to have a sort of consensus algorithm in order to ensure that only the leader performs the backup.

There is no need of a consensus algorithm since Patroni already elect the primary based on a consensus algorithm. The controller will just ask Patroni if current Pod is the primary before starting any backup. We have then to check who is the primary after the backup, and, if the backup completes and the primary Pod changed discard such backup by marking it as failed. To be extra sure we may use the Patroni history so that even for long backups we can make sure the primary did not changed at all (like failover to another Pod and then failover back to the current one).

# Side note

Current implementation was affected by a bug were a client-side throttling was applied by the `kubectl` command due to the user not having permissions to write in the home `$HOME` directory. This should be fixed by #1552 (!1051). This may improve performance considerably, but we should test on clouds.

apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1

  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  persistentVolume:
    size: 100Gi
```

    sgDistributedLogs: 'monitoring.distributedlogs'
    retention: "15 days"
```

What we need to fix here, is the link on the "Cluster Details" table, which assumes the logs server is always on the same namespace even though that's not always the case.
