Issue:
Change the default `idle_timeout` option on `TcpProxy` filter for EnvoyProxy
The default [`idle_timeout`](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.15.0/api-v3/extensions/filters/network/tcp_proxy/v3/tcp_proxy.proto#envoy-v3-api-field-extensions-filters-network-tcp-proxy-v3-tcpproxy-idle-timeout) setting on TcpProxy filter is 1 hour, so if some user query spend more than one hour to finish the EnvoyProxy will finish the connection by timeout, because the EnvoyProxy don't have the notion that the connection actually is not idle but waiting for processing the query instead.

Change the `idle_timeout` value to be `0` for all TCP proxy of Envoy configurations.

[DISCUSSION]
[fabrizio.ongres]: Did some tests to confirm it and set the `idle_timeout=10s` and ran `SELECT pg_sleep(20)` on Postgres, so the Envoy finished the connection as expected:

```

[2020-09-01 11:56:30.299][27755][debug][pool] [external/envoy/source/common/tcp/original_conn_pool.cc:255] [C3] connection destroyed
```

And on Postgres psql session:

```
fabrizio=# select pg_sleep(20);
server closed the connection unexpectedly
	This probably means the server terminated abnormally
	before or while processing the request.
```

[fabrizio.ongres]: One option is disable it completely by setting to 0 (zero). Doing that I'm just wondering if we'll face some problems on the Envoy side by leaking connections.

[sebawebber]: I think that we can keep the default (1h) and let the user define the appropriate value. That option will bring the possibility to make SG more flexible for different kinds of environments.

[ahachete]: My vote is to completely disable it, and include this fix for `0.9.1`. I won't object to expose this to the CRD as an optional advanced usage, it undoubtedly adds some value and gives the PG DBA more weapons, but that would be `1.0` stuff.

Conceptually, Envoy proxy is meant to be fully transparent. If it can kill a long-running query, without the user expecting that, it is no longer transparent.

As of now, this default value kills long-running queries. What do I do if I want to run long reports? Two days ago I run a query that took 12h. It would have been killed, and then what do I do? There's no workaround.

I would disable it. If that would at some later point introduce other problems, is something we might need to consider (then) and/or test/infer (before).

[teoincontatto]: If we terminate the connection on the pg side with `pg_terminate_backend(<pid>)` then it will probably leak connection on the envoy side as long as the client does not support a timeout. But:

* This is actually not a common behavior or best practice to close a connection. We could document that and ask for that case to use `pg_cancel_backend(<pid>)`
* In any case the connection is leaked only until the client closes it so this can be fixed from the client.
* Probably we could add some feature in the future to close those leaked connections.

[teoincontatto]: And to make ti clear I am for disable it completely (`idle_timeout`=0).

[sebawebber]: about the `pg_terminate_backend()`, do we have any testing about that? this is something that will occour with frequency.

[fabrizio.ongres]: Already merged

Issue:
pg_rewind/pg_basebackup is waiting on a checkpoint from the master
On a recent e2e test on EKS, it was found that after killing the master, another pod was elected master and the new pod (attached to the PV of the old master) was not being brought up. Upon container log inspection, it was found waiting on `pg_rewind` which in turn was waiting on a checkpoint from the new master. The probe was reporting the container as unhealthy.

With a manual `CHECKPOINT` command on the master, the (new replica, old master) was able to proceed successfully. So we need to answer the following questions:

*  Does `pg_rewind` needs to forcibly wait for a checkpoint on the master?
*  Is there any way for `pg_rewind` to for the checkpoint by itself?
*  Any other better alternative than forcing very low [checkpoint_timeout](https://postgresqlco.nf/en/doc/param/checkpoint_timeout) on our end?

The same effect may happen when initializing a replica from a `pg_basebackup`.

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: Check if is possible to configure patroni (with a hook?!) in order to send a checkpoint to the elected master when a replica has joined the cluster.

[teoincontatto]: Since this is happening because of a high `checkpoint_timeout` we consider changing this to a lower value (30s) in the demo configuration of the cluster in order to avoid this problem.

> When executing pg_rewind using an online cluster as source which has been recently promoted, it is necessary to execute a CHECKPOINT after promotion so as its control file reflects up-to-date timeline information, which is used by pg_rewind to check if the target cluster can be rewound using the designated source cluster.

See https://www.postgresql.org/docs/11/app-pgrewind.html

[sergio.ostapowicz]: I have seen the value for the demo, but forcing Postgres to flush WALS each 30s is not a good approach. 

We can't use that option for a production installation. The default value in pg12 is 5min and is half from very busy production servers. We need to rollback that value (but I know that the idea is to remove the demo from there)

[ahachete]: The same happens with `pg_basebackup`, called by Patroni. Until a `CHECKPOINT` happens in the master, the command is stuck. Doing a manual one fixes it quicker.

This is an important issue, it leads to replicas taking even minutes to be brought up, unless a manual checkpoint is run.

But it doesn't appear in the config documentation or how to set or if it's enabled by default neither.
Despite of that, I have [researched in the code](https://github.com/zalando/patroni/blob/e87fc12aebc6eb15b5efce3a10181c032b0e9965/patroni/postgresql/rewind.py#L231) and it looks like the CHECKPOINT always run after node promotion:

```py
    def ensure_checkpoint_after_promote(self, wakeup):
        """After promote issue a CHECKPOINT from a new thread and asynchronously check the result.
        In case if CHECKPOINT failed, just check that timeline in pg_control was updated."""

        if self._state == REWIND_STATUS.INITIAL and self._postgresql.is_leader():
            with self._checkpoint_task_lock:
                if self._checkpoint_task:
                    with self._checkpoint_task:
                        if self._checkpoint_task.result:
                            self._state = REWIND_STATUS.CHECKPOINT
                        if self._checkpoint_task.result is not False:
                            return
                else:
                    self._checkpoint_task = CriticalTask()
                    return Thread(target=self.__checkpoint, args=(self._checkpoint_task, wakeup)).start()

            if self._postgresql.get_master_timeline() == self._postgresql.pg_control_timeline():
                self._state = REWIND_STATUS.CHECKPOINT

    def checkpoint_after_promote(self):
        return self._state == REWIND_STATUS.CHECKPOINT
```
Therefore, we could conclude that using the last Patroni version on SG solves the problem.

[ahachete]: I have further researched this a bit. There are three separate topics.

**Spreading the instances across all available zones/AZs**.

This is, in theory, done [automatically, at least on AWS and GKE](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/best-practices/multiple-zones/). The way it works is by the cloud provider filling in the [failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/labels-annotations-taints/#failure-domainbetakubernetesiozone) (deprecated in `1.17`) or [topology.kubernetes.io/zone](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/labels-annotations-taints/#topologykubernetesiozone) (since `1.17`) labels on the nodes. When a `StatefulSet` requires some PVCs, they are automatically spread through the different values of these labels.

However:

> This is achieved via SelectorSpreadPriority.
    SelectorSpreadPriority is a best effort placement. If the zones in your cluster are heterogeneous (for example: different numbers of nodes, different types of nodes, or different pod resource requirements), this placement might prevent equal spreading of your Pods across zones. If desired, you can use homogenous zones (same number and types of nodes) to reduce the probability of unequal spreading.

I have tested this with `1.14` on `AWS`. I used 4 nodes distributed across 3 AZs, and then created a `SGCluster` of 3 instances. 2 of them ended up in the same AZ, while 1 AZ had no instances. We can see this clearly in how the PVCs/PVs are created, which is actually what determines the pod placement in the nodes:

```
kubectl get pv --show-labels
NAME                                       CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM                    STORAGECLASS   REASON   AGE    LABELS
pvc-0ea8b68a-7f50-11ea-b9ac-0e748dd2e2a6   10Gi       RWO            Delete           Bound    default/sg1-data-sg1-0   gp2                     152m   failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/region=eu-west-3,failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone=eu-west-3b
pvc-2d5d504c-7f50-11ea-b9ac-0e748dd2e2a6   10Gi       RWO            Delete           Bound    default/sg1-data-sg1-1   gp2                     151m   failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/region=eu-west-3,failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone=eu-west-3c
pvc-48354aab-7f50-11ea-b9ac-0e748dd2e2a6   10Gi       RWO            Delete           Bound    default/sg1-data-sg1-2   gp2                     150m   failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/region=eu-west-3,failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone=eu-west-3c
```

Further investigation will be required here. However, we may consider this default behaviour as "good for now", as while not perfect, it tries to provide some spreading, and I'm not sure as of now how to improve this --other than writing our own equivalent to the `StatefulSet`.


**Enforcing the one pod per node best practice**.

We should give a detail look at the post "[How to deploy a Statefulset where you get one pod per node (like a Daemonset) StatefulDaemonSet](https://medium.com/@johnjjung/building-a-kubernetes-daemonstatefulset-30ad0592d8cb)". This may be a better alternative to our current anti-affinity rule.


**Passing arbitrary node selectors to the pods**.

This could also be implemented, as long as it doesn't conflict with the above. [ahachete]: Analyzing this topic again, I would like to reinforce its importance and add another related concept: [node tolerations](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/).

From a 30,000 feet perspective, what we want is to enforce by default, or help enforce, best practices of how databases are run in production on enterprise-grade environments. In most cases, this means dedicated nodes. There are three aspects of this, with only one addressed so far in SG:

1.  PodAntiAffinity. This prevents (by default, as can be disabled) two SG pods to be run on the same node.
1.  Node selectors and/or node affinity. Both target declarative selection on which nodes can SG pods be run.
1.  Node tolerations. They allow pods to be run on nodes which are potentially restricted from execution for other pods.

Basically, 1 is needed to prevent two or more pods to run on the same node; 2 is the most powerful way (specially node affinity) to declare where SG pods need to run; and 3 is potentially also needed to ensure nodes are effectively dedicated, i.e., only SG pods would run there.

IOW, we need to implement all three to be able to support the concept of a "dedicated node" (combination of 1 and 3) and that we can select quite precisely which node (or class of nodes) that dedicated node is (2).

Issue:
Add cluster namespace and name labels to postgres-exporter metrics
Currently postgres-exporter metrics does not have custom labels for metrics. In order to be able to identify from what StackGres cluster those metrics are, it's necessary to add some constant labels. 

An example of one of the current metrics:

```
# HELP pg_stat_activity_count number of connections in this state
# TYPE pg_stat_activity_count gauge
pg_stat_activity_count{datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="active"} 1
pg_stat_activity_count{datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="disabled"} 0
pg_stat_activity_count{datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="fastpath function call"} 0
pg_stat_activity_count{datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="idle"} 1
```

The labels suggested to be added are: `cluster_name` and `namespace` so the metrics will look like:

```
# HELP pg_stat_activity_count number of connections in this state
# TYPE pg_stat_activity_count gauge
pg_stat_activity_count{cluster_name="my_cluster",namespace="my_namespace",datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="active"} 1
pg_stat_activity_count{cluster_name="my_cluster",namespace="my_namespace",datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="disabled"} 0
pg_stat_activity_count{cluster_name="my_cluster",namespace="my_namespace",datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="fastpath function call"} 0
pg_stat_activity_count{cluster_name="my_cluster",namespace="my_namespace",datname="postgres",server="localhost:5432",state="idle"} 1
```

In some environments with multiple clusters will be more easy to identify where those metrics come from.

To add these metrics to the postgres-exporter is necesary to configure this next parameter:

```
PG_EXPORTER_CONSTANT_LABELS="cluster_name=MY_CLUSTER, namespace=MY_NAMESPACE"
```

```

3- Generate logs with `pgbadger` format (example: using log_time filter)
 ``` 
kubectl exec -it -n sg-pre $POD_NAME -c patroni -- psql -d databasename -c "copy (SELECT     log_time, user_name  ,database_name ,process_id ,connection_from ,session_id ,session_line_num ,command_tag ,session_start_time ,virtual_transaction_id ,transaction_id , error_severity,sql_state_code ,message,detail ,hint ,internal_query ,internal_query_pos ,context ,query ,query_pos ,"location" ,application_name FROM log_postgres lp where  log_time >'begin timestamp' and log_time <'end timestamp') to '/tmp/log_formatted.csv' CSV DELIMITER ',';"
```

4- Bring the logs to your host (is there another a bit more fancy way to bring the file?)
```
kubectl exec -it -n sg-pre $POD_NAME -c patroni -- cat /tmp/log_formatted.csv > log_formatted.csv
```


5- Analyze the logs with `pgbadger`
```
pgbadger  -f csv -o pgbadger_report.html log_formatted.csv
```

Issue:
Design and implement the UI to consult centralized logs
StackGres `0.9` is adding the functionality to aggregate all the PostgreSQL (and Patroni) logs on a central location. We need to have an UI in the web to show these centralized logs. The underlying system where these logs are going to be stored is based on Postgres, and hence we can query in SQL (although this would be provided by a Web Service that exposes this to the UI). But this means we have a lot of powerful operations to query and obtain the log information from the central location.

The goal of this issue is to design how this UI would look like. Some of the criteria that needs to be taken into account are the following:

*  Essentially, the UI should present a "single table query results" interface, where you can filter by some fields and potentially order by other fields.
*  All logs will have a first field which is a timestamp, and this is the main ordering criteria. Logs are ordered by time, and this time information should be clear information and potentially the first field.
*  We might want to separate Postgres logs from Patroni logs as different tables / views or all together in the same place. This is not decided yet.
*  By default, the most recent logs are to be shown. User may be able to specify time ranges over what timeframe she wants the logs to be shown. "Convenience" buttons/shortcuts should be provided for usual cases (last 5 minutes, last 30 minutes, last 1h, last 3h, last day, etc).
*  Information volume may be huge. At most XXX logs should be shown in the screen, with potentially the option to paginate them.
*  In general logs are unstructured information, and may contain different data types on each line. But some fields will be always present and probably extracted as separated columns. These separate columns may be used for filtering and ordering. For example, the particular server from which the log comes. The user should be able to either filter and only see logs from a particular server, or see them all but ordered by this field. A possible initial set of fixed log fields could be:
    *  Timestamp
    *  Log type (`Postgres` or `Patroni`).
    *  Pod name (server name)
    *  Replication status (either `Master` or `Replica`)
    *  Error criticality. All values to be determined, but as an initial idea: `FATAL`, `ERROR`, `WARNING`, `INFO`, `DEBUG`. The values of this field may actually lead to different colouring of the row for this log.
*  The rest of the log information (i.e. non-fixed fields) may be presented raw, but maybe we will identify some patterns within to highlight particular cases of logs.
*  A free-text field for searching for log information is required.
*  As some of the example UI log visualizing systems mentioned below do, it could be interesting to show a graph on top of the log results with the number of log events per day, where you can easily click on any bar and that automatically selects a given day. This could be postponed to a second version of this UI interface.

Grafana dashboard shows replication lag but there is no lag
### Summary

Grafana dashboard shows replication lag.

![image](/uploads/dccaef8741ca24bed000b3a5048cc645/image.png)

But from patroni side there's not replication lag:

```
+ Cluster: mminventory (6885621283419865177) --+---------+----+-----------+
|     Member    |         Host        |  Role  |  State  | TL | Lag in MB |
+---------------+---------------------+--------+---------+----+-----------+
| mminventory-0 | 10.192.146.203:7433 | Leader | running |  9 |           |
| mminventory-1 |  10.192.146.69:7433 |        | running |  9 |         0 |
| mminventory-2 |  10.192.146.44:7433 |        | running |  9 |         0 |
+---------------+---------------------+--------+---------+----+-----------+
```

### Current Behaviour 

When a cluster has no much activity the replication lag metrics start to show an increment in the replication lag but at database level there is not. 

#### Steps to reproduce

If the database cluster has a low activity and the due to this the last transaction replayed during recovery does not change quickly is when the metric start to show replication lag.  

### Expected Behaviour

Even when the database cluster has not much activity the metric should not show that there is replication lag, this means that the metric has something wrong. 

### Possible Solution

Change the current metric query: 

```
SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp())) as lag, CASE WHEN pg_is_in_recovery() THEN 1 ELSE 0 END as is_replica
```

To:

```
select
    case
      when pg_last_wal_receive_lsn() = pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() then 0
      else extract (EPOCH FROM now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp())::integer
    end as lag,
    case
      when pg_is_in_recovery() then 1
      else 0
    end as is_replica;
```

*  Applies only when a user creates a CR of kind `SGDistributedLogs`:
    *  [ ] Spin a pod with Fluentd. This instance should also receive the appropriate Fluentd configuration from a ConfigMap. It will collect the logs from every FluentBit. This pod needs to be HA, so possibly deployed as a Deployment with size=1. Should also possibly expose itself as a service, so that FluentBits locate it easily when talking to it.
    *  [ ] Spin a "reduced" StackGres cluster, with the following characteristics:

        *  Just a single sidecar that will contain Fluentd. This instance should also receive the appropriate Fluentd configuration from a ConfigMap. It will collect the logs from every FluentBit. Should also possibly expose itself as a service, so that FluentBits locate it easily when talking to it.
        *  TimescaleDB extension (open source version) included.
        *  Given schema for the database already created. See #182

[teoincontatto]: Here a brief guide to set up minishift to run StackGres on a Linux system (tested on Ubuntu 18.04):

First install minishift:

* The virtualization environment to run minishift on Linux is KVM as described in official doc: https://docs.okd.io/3.11/minishift/getting-started/setting-up-virtualization-environment.html
* Download and install the minishift executable so it can be executed from a terminal: https://github.com/minishift/minishift/releases

Second start and configure minishift:

1. Start minishift. Set CPU, memory and disk according to your environment. The minimum recommended is 2 CPU, 4GB and 20GB

```
  K8S_OPENSHIFT_VERSION=3.11.0
  K8S_MINISHIFT_CPUS=2
  K8S_MINISHIFT_MEMORY=4GB
  K8S_MINISHIFT_DISK=20GB
  K8S_MINISHIFT_VMDRIVER=kvm
  minishift start --openshift-version "v$K8S_OPENSHIFT_VERSION" \
    --cpus "$K8S_MINISHIFT_CPUS" \
    --memory "$K8S_MINISHIFT_MEMORY" \
    --disk-size "$K8S_MINISHIFT_DISK" \
    --vm-driver "$K8S_MINISHIFT_VMDRIVER"
```

2. Check minishift is up and running by logging in with `oc`:

```
  eval "$(minishift oc-env)"

  if ! timeout -s KILL 10s oc login -u system:admin > /dev/null 2>&1
  then
    minishift status | grep '^OpenShift:  Running '
    timeout -s KILL 180s eval 'until timeout -s KILL 10s oc login -u system:admin > /dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done'
  fi
```

3. Apply patches in order to fix a [minishift bug](https://github.com/minishift/minishift/issues/3290) and enable `PodShareProcessNamespace` feature gate:

```
  (
  set -e
  local OPENSHIFT_TARGET
  for OPENSHIFT_TARGET in kube node master
  do
    # Workaround for https://github.com/minishift/minishift/issues/3290
    minishift openshift config view --target="$OPENSHIFT_TARGET" \
      | grep -A 1 'cluster-signing-cert-file:' | grep -q '/etc/origin/master/ca.crt' \
      || minishift openshift config set --target="$OPENSHIFT_TARGET" --patch '{
        "kubernetesMasterConfig": {
          "controllerArguments": {
            "cluster-signing-cert-file": ["/etc/origin/master/ca.crt"],
            "cluster-signing-key-file": ["/etc/origin/master/ca.key"],
            "feature-gates": ["PodShareProcessNamespace=true"]
          },
          "apiServerArguments": {
            "feature-gates":  ["PodShareProcessNamespace=true"]
          }
        },
        "kubeletArguments": {
          "feature-gates": ["PodShareProcessNamespace=true"]
        }
      }'

    if ! timeout -s KILL 10s oc login -u system:admin > /dev/null 2>&1
    then
      timeout -s KILL 180s eval 'until timeout -s KILL 10s oc login -u system:admin > /dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done'
    fi
  done

  if ! minishift ssh -- ps -ef | grep '[k]ubelet' | grep -q 'PodShareProcessNamespace=true'
  then
    minishift stop
    minishift start
    if ! timeout -s KILL 10s oc login -u system:admin > /dev/null 2>&1
    then
      minishift status | grep '^OpenShift:  Running '
      timeout -s KILL 180s eval 'until timeout -s KILL 10s oc login -u system:admin > /dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done'
    fi
  fi
 )
```

4. Install minishift add-on to enable admission webhooks:

```
  for addon in admissions-webhook
  do
    minishift addons list | grep -q "^- $addon\s\+: enabled\s" \
     || ( minishift addons enable "$addon" && minishift addons apply "$addon" \

        then
          timeout -s KILL 180s eval 'until timeout -s KILL 10s oc login -u system:admin > /dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done'
        fi )
  done
```

[jorsol]: Here a brief guide to set up OpenShift 3.11 single node to test StackGres:

First: install openshift 3.11:

* Create a VM with CentOS 7 (on AWS).
* SSH login to the VM.
* `sudo yum install git`
* Install the openshift script from this repository: 
  * `git clone https://github.com/okd-community-install/installcentos.git`
* `cd installcentos; sudo ./install-openshift.sh`
* Follow the instructions on the script.

Second: configure openshift:

* As root, edit the file: `/etc/origin/master/master-config.yaml`
* Here we need to enable the admision-webhooks in admisionConfig section:
```
admissionConfig:
  pluginConfig:
    ValidatingAdmissionWebhook:
      configuration:
        apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
        kind: WebhookAdmission
        kubeConfigFile: /dev/null
    MutatingAdmissionWebhook:
      configuration:
        apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
        kind: WebhookAdmission
        kubeConfigFile: /dev/null
   ...
```
* Also we need to enable `PodShareProcessNamespace` feature gate, search the kubernetesMasterConfig section and add the feature gate to apiServerArguments and controllerArguments, it will look like this:
```
kubernetesMasterConfig:
  apiServerArguments:
    ...
    feature-gates:
    - PodShareProcessNamespace=true
  controllerArguments:
    ...
    feature-gates:
    - PodShareProcessNamespace=true
```

* Allow to run container as root and allows host mounts and any UID by a pod (this last is needed to make by the persistent volume recycler of minishift to work and not fail when a PV is released).

```
  oc adm policy add-scc-to-group anyuid system:authenticated
  oc adm policy add-scc-to-group hostmount-anyuid system:serviceaccounts
```

This cluster creates PV with Reclaim policy, we probably need to change the policy to Recycle so that way the PV can be reused on other tests, there are 200 PV created by openshift, one way to change the policy is:

```for i in {1..200}; do kubectl patch pv vol$i --patch '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Recycle"}}'; done;```

Now test the e2e like:

```
E2E_ENV=openshift E2E_OPERATOR_PULL_POLICY=Always E2E_PARALLELISM=1 K8S_REUSE=true E2E_REUSE_OPERATOR=false E2E_BUILD_OPERATOR=false E2E_SKIP_SETUP=false E2E_SKIP_OPERATOR_LOAD=true E2E_DISABLE_FAST_CLEANUP=true bash -x stackgres-k8s/e2e/run-test.sh stackgres-k8s/e2e/spec/connectivity
```

To run all the test try with the script: `stackgres-k8s/e2e/run-all-test.sh`

Issue:
Make all container able to run as an arbitrary user ID (non-root)
### Problem to solve

A container should never run as root user since it is a security flaw.

The operator currently runs the postgres image and other images as a fixed user id, this caused some problems on more restricted environments like openshift.

### Further details

Kubernetes compatible platform like [OpenShift](https://github.com/minishift/minishift/issues/3290#issuecomment-535439518) disallow run a container as root by default.

The best solution is to build the application image so it can be run as an arbitrary user ID. This avoids the risks associated with having to run an application as the root user ID, or other fixed user ID which may be shared with applications in other projects.

### Proposal

Make all containers spawned by StackGres helm charts and operator run with non-root user.

### Testing

The filesystem permissions could be tricky to work with, so this should test some combination of deleting pods, changing pvc, etc.

### Links / references

* https://dev.to/techworld_with_nana/run-pod-with-root-privileges-41n9
* https://opensource.com/article/18/3/just-say-no-root-containers
* https://www.openshift.com/blog/jupyter-on-openshift-part-6-running-as-an-assigned-user-id
* https://cookbook.openshift.org/users-and-role-based-access-control/how-can-i-enable-an-image-to-run-as-a-set-user-id.html

[DISCUSSION]

For k8s 1.11 it will no longer be possible to run tests and for 1.12, 1.14 and 1.16 some test are failing (since service DNS are not working).

I've tried all latest k8s versions with kind 0.7.0 and they all works. If at some point someone need to upgrade kind for some reason we will have to drop support for k8s 1.11 (but we still can maintain support for openshift 3.6 by testing with minishift) and will also need to check that mentioned upstream issue related to coredns error has been fixed.

Seems that kind 0.8.1 is not broken but the way we are using the tool is wrong (at least not stable). It was clearly stated in the kind release page (but not in the documentation) that images to use for a specific kind version have the k8s version in the tag and are built with a specific sha. Seems that kind overwrite on purpose the tag with a different sha whan a new kind version is released.

[teoincontatto]: So, the current solution adopted is to copy the `/etc/(passwd|group|shadow|gshadow)` files to an empty dir (disk backed) using an init container and add the user to those files with the UID and GID assigned by openshift at runtime. We then mount the file as read-only on the containers.

The trick is only required in openshift and is enabled using the operator environment variable `USE_ARBITRARY_USER`.

[ahachete]: Even if it is only required in OpenShift, are we performing it always (controlled by the env variable?). Because it's probably not a bad practice anyway, so may be a sensible default (even though is a bit of a trick, as you mentioned).

[teoincontatto]: > Even if it is only required in OpenShift, are we performing it always (controlled by the env variable?). Because it's probably not a bad practice anyway, so may be a sensible default (even though is a bit of a trick, as you mentioned).

We could share the generation and use of `/etc/(passwd|group|shadow|gshadow)` files but we still need `USE_ARBITRARY_USER` environment variable to avoid defining `runAsuser`, `runAsGroup` and `fsGroup` when running on openshift.

Openshift overwrite the container user and group with an arbitrary user if no `runAsuser`, `runAsGroup` or `fsGroup` are defined in section `securityContext` of the pod. And if defined it is required a [Security Context Constraint](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.6/admin_guide/manage_scc.html) to avoid the error like:

```
Error creating: pods "stackgres-operator-8584449745-" is forbidden: unable to validate against any security context constraint: [fsGroup: Invalid value: []int64{999}: 999 is not an allowed group spec.containers[0].securityContext.securityContext.runAsUser: Invalid value: 999: must be in the ranges: [1000130000, 1000139999] spec.containers[1].securityContext.securityContext.runAsUser: Invalid value: 999: must be in the ranges: [1000130000, 1000139999]]
```

Instead, vanilla kubernetes requires to specify the group for the `fsGroup` parameter of the `securityContext` of the pod or we will not be able to write to the PV.

> Is this being combined with [Security context](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/)s?

Yes!

In a previous discussion I thought emptyDir was backed only by memory but after reviewing documentation the default is not the memory but the node disk:

> By default, emptyDir volumes are stored on whatever medium is backing the node - that might be disk or SSD or network storage, depending on your environment. However, you can set the emptyDir.medium field to "Memory" to tell Kubernetes to mount a tmpfs (RAM-backed filesystem) for you instead. While tmpfs is very fast, be aware that unlike disks, tmpfs is cleared on node reboot and any files you write will count against your Container’s memory limit.

This mean that the mentioned workaround is a viable and probably more correct way to read log files from another container.

Meaning that it is possible that a the same PV can be mounted in multiple container of the same pod since all of them will be running in the same node.

[ahachete]: I can confirm it works, at least on the two environments that I have tested: `microk8s` and `EKS`. This is the YAML used:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: myclaim
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: mypod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: c1
      image: ubuntu
      command: ["tail", "-f", "/dev/null"]
      volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: "/tmp/c1"
        name: mypd
    - name: c2
      image: ubuntu
      command: ["tail", "-f", "/dev/null"]
      volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: "/tmp/c2"
        name: mypd
        readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: mypd
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: myclaim
```

[xaviersierra]: After a few days of investigation, I've found that this issue is caused by the [storage version migrator](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kube-storage-version-migrator/blob/master/USER_GUIDE.md). In short, its a kubernetes componentent that makes sure that all objects stored in etcd are compatible with to the latest API server of the kubernetes cluster. In order to fullfil this purpose, every 10 minutes, the storage version migrator checks all stored objects and migrates them. 

The problem comes when the storage version migrator tries to migrate stackgres's default custom resources. Those resources are proteccted against update by default, to enforce that we have settled a couple valiadation webhooks that checks that no defautl CR is updated.

When the storage version migrator is doing it's migration process, it triggers an update over all CRs that it migrates, that is rejected by the admission webhook. Even though that the storage version migrator doesn't update the content of CR it still triggers an update. This update, then is rejected by the validating admission webhook. 

When the update is rejected, storage version migration doesn't move forward, instead it got stuck in an endless loop of retrials that it will only stop once it can successfully do the update. 

I will submit a fix on the validation webhooks so it allow the updates that comes from the storage vesion migrator,

# CPU

The CPU count from `cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep '^processor' | wc -l` is the CPU count of the host. In a cgroup we can calculate the CPU assigned with:

  * container cpu quota: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us`
  * container cpu period: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us`

So: container cpus = container cpu quota / container cpu period

A corner case is when cpu quota is -1. In that case: container cpus = host cpus

The memory from `cat /proc/meminfo|grep "^MemTotal:"|sed 's/\\s\\+/ /g'|cut -d ' ' -f 2` and `cat /proc/meminfo|grep "^MemAvailable:"|sed 's/\\s\\+/ /g'|cut -d ' ' -f 2` is the memory total and available of the host. In a cgroup we can obtain total and rss (used excluding cache) memory with:

  * total memory: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.max_usage_in_bytes`
  * used memory: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.stat | grep '^total_rss ' | cut -d ' ' -f 2`

# Load average

I did not found a way to get a container loadavg similar to the one that can be obtained from `cat /proc/loadavg` so this will refer as a node usage stat.

Issue:
Switch to emptyDir for distributed logs
To avoid the need to use ShareProcessNamespace feature gate (see #359) we want to switch from storing logs to an emptyDir backed by node local storage when distributed logs is enabled in a cluster.

Currently fluent-bit reads the logs from the file system of the patroni process using the path `/proc/<patroni pid>/root/...`. Using an emptyDir is a much better approach since the path becomes static instead of dynamic.

[DISCUSSION]
[jorsol]: I'm not familiar with current implementation of distributed logs... but a best practice is to limit usage of log forwarders in a sidecar pattern, as they will utilize a lot more resources. The option is to use a DaemonSet for the log forwarder and sending logs to STDOUT.

[teoincontatto]: When this was implemented DeamonSet seems a good option to me. But the problems of using DeamonSet by retrieving logs from STDOUT were:

* It could be error prone to separate logs from Patroni and Postgres (consider multi line logs).
* We choosed to use the CSV log collector to have the Postgres logs already parsed at the source.

Implementing a parser from scratch that solve those two points is a considerable effort.

On the other side, if you consider a production installation, we force (using an anti-affinity rule) a k8s node to have a single StackGres cluster's Pod. So we end up having a pattern that is the same as using a DeamonSet.

[jorsol]: The anti-affinity rule is great, but that's assuming that all environments will have a single cluster (of SG), there is another pattern that you can have multiple application in a single cluster, and it's not a bad thing either.

The extreme case is a microservice architecture where every single domain has a database on it's own.

[teoincontatto]: By writing "environments" and "domains" are you referring to namespaces?

[jorsol]: Bad choice of words, by "environment" I mean Production/Staging/Development (or in other words, a K8s cluster), and by "domain" I mean the "business domain" or "bounded context" of the application.

[teoincontatto]: > The anti-affinity rule is great, but that's assuming that all environments will have a single cluster (of SG), there is another pattern that you can have multiple application in a single cluster, and it's not a bad thing either.

We enforce our users to have a single SG cluster pod per node (at least in a production environment). We do not assume a single SG cluster for each environment but we enforce that each environment have dedicated node for each SG cluster pod.

The rule is not perfect and an user can have multiple SG cluster pod in the same node for different namespaces. That is a case that we would like to avoid but anti affinity rules can not prevent it. IMHO we should allow a user to accept drawbacks of running more SG cluster pods on the same node if she has requirements to fulfill. We added custom labels and annotations to allow the user to make a more fine grained distribution of SG cluster pod. Probably we should allow to add custom affinity rules to have even more control on that.

> The extreme case is a microservice architecture where every single domain has a database on it's own.

Still, no problem with that but to use SG "the right (and opinionated) way" you will need a k8s dedicated node for each SG cluster pod or take the decision to not follow that rule accepting all the drawbacks.

[ahachete]: I think the approach described here is the best possible one so far. To summarize:

*  Advantages:
    * We avoid needing to use share process namespace.
    * We avoid needing to find the dynamic path on which log files are.
    * We leverage Postgres rich CSV logging format.
    * We still have persistance, shared across the two pods.
*  Disadvantages:
    * We may have several sidecars for log collection on a given node. However, I don't see this as a big deal as a) we still recommend to have one SGCluster per node, as mentioned above; and if this is not the case, this becomes some duplication of resources, but that's about it. Alternatives would require more complex scenarios or preventing the use of the rich CSV log format.

Going the DaemonSet route is something we might consider later and with a wider scope, as it may affect other areas too (e.g. sending monitoring information, or even connection pooling). But that's a significantly bigger discussion.

[NikolayS]: My several cents:

`default_statistics_target = 200` -- very interesting, why?

`random_page_cost` – Why 1.5? Is random access expected to be so slower than sequential nowadays?

`huge_pages` - why `off`? Why not default `try`?

`max_wal_size = max(2GB, $shared_buffers \* 2)` – interesting approach. Trying to understand the reasons. If I have 1 TiB of RAM and not very fast disks (EBS or PD, for example), and use 800 GiB of RAM for `shared_buffers`, then I'll have `max_wal_size = 1.6 TiB`? It effectively means `max_wal_size = ∞`.

`pg_stat_statements.track` – I would be careful here. Do you think that it's what is better in most cases? It affects pg_stat_statements' content and may complicate analysis.

As for pg_stat_statements, I would do `pg_stat_statements.track_utility = off` – in my experience, analyzing of SETs is not useful in 99.99% cases, while it affects the performance of pg_stat_statements.

`maintenance_work_mem = min(2GB, max(64MB, $Ram / 8))` – it may be too much. Again, if I have 1 TiB of RAM, I wouldn't want to dedicate 1/8 of it to `maintenance_work_mem`, meaning that CREATE INDEX of a large index would wash out a significant amount of useful cache. And autovacuum.. (BTW, what is `autovacuum_work_mem`? Default -1? So multiple workers would make this problem bigger). My experiments I did last year showed that large `maintenance_work_mem` do not really improve index creation timing – when you jump from '100 MiB' to `500 MiB` the increase is noticeable, but from `500 MiB` to `1 GiB` and `2 GiB` it's already not really big, which is not we usually think. Of course, more experiments would be helpful here.

Autovacuum settings are ones of the most important to tune - do you plan to touch them?

We've discussed around it and although the sequential and random access have almost the same speed on modern disks it still have a bit of difference so we decide to give a more conservative value but better than the default 4 (old for magnetic).

Nowadays using EBS (gp2 or io1) on AWS I generally use `random_page_cost=1.1` for the all instances I have opportunity to touch.

[ahachete]: So we're trying here to strike a delicate balance: on one side, we want to provide more "common" values for the vast majority of users, rather than the (sometimes) overly conservative Postgres default values. On the other side, all these values can be overridden by the user, but we know they should be still conservative and not lead to very bad practices if not overridden, as we anticipate is most of the time the case.

So we can take a bit more involved tuning on some parameters, but at the same time we still keep some headroom for conservativeness. `random_page_cost=1.5` is a great example here: default value is good for those with magnetic disks. But K8s users are unlikely to run on them, so we're good making it closer to 1. But at the same time, something like `1` or `1.1` would not work that well for the remaining cases where magnetic disks are used, or somewhat networked disks still perform better with sequential throughout. Thus, even if not perfect, `1.5` is a middle-ground between providing good optimization for most, while not hurting the rest.

Having said that, thank you for your comments, we will review the parameters based on this. As for autovacuum it's really hard, as it is too much workload dependent and I believe we can't hardcode strong opinions here.

About `huge_pages`: `try` is normally a bad choice, even in non-containerized environments, as the THPs that most Linux systems may have, have really bad performance. But even then, in K8s you need to specify specific limits and resource requests if you plan to use HPs, so this belongs to a whole new story. For now, we assume no HPs are used and therefore stick with `off`. But, again, as a user, you may happily override this value.

[jorsol]: What about the SSL/TLS configuration parameters?

I would enable a sensible default, for TLS that finish on envoy, the connection could be plain, but for connection between replicas (or for full encryption even with envoy), I would definitely want to enable TLS.

The minimum configuration could be:
```
ssl = on

ssl_cert_file = '/path/to/signed_cert_plus_intermediates'
ssl_key_file = '/path/to/private_key'

ssl_dh_params_file = '/path/to/dhparam'

ssl_ciphers = 'ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305'
ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.2'
```

The `ssl_min_protocol_version` applies to Postgres 12+ and for Postgres 12+, the ciphers are for ECC certificates that could be created by the operator.

Issue:
Create a backup CRD to enable record and delete real backups
Create a backup CRD that will store information of a real backup.

A creation backup Job will be started by the operator each time a backup CR is created (without a state) putting it's phase as "pending". The operator will set the backup CR as the owner of the creation backup Job.

The creation backup Job will set the Pod name that is creating the backup. When the backup completes the Job will update the backup CR phase to "completed" and will add all the backup information. Ideally the backup should include LSN, timestamp of the backup for PITR and the backup size and the timestamp of backup completion. On any error the Job will set the reason of the error and set the phase of backup CR to "failed".

The creation backup Job will also perform the retention cleanup after creating the backup and the cleanup of CRs associated to those backups that where removed by the retention cleanup.

The logic to allow one CronJob to execute at a time will be replicated in the creation backup Job so that only one creation backup Job will be able to run at a time. 

The CronJob that is creating full backups will create a new backup CR with the state of "pending" that will not make the operator spawn a new creation backup Job. Instead the Job created by the CronJob will operate as a creation backup Job (also using the same lock so that will be executed a single backup at any time). This approach will enforce that the scheduled backup will be generated even if the operator is out of service or removed.

[DISCUSSION]

[teoincontatto]: A cluster CR define a `sidecars` as an array of strings, each representing a container in the pod that provide some functionality. The main container is patroni+postgresql and is not optional. There are also two more containers (envoy and postgres-exporter) that are also non optional and are added by default no matter if thay are specified in the `sidecars` array or not. Also the connection-pooling sidecar requires to define a configuration in the `connectionPoolingConfig` field (the requirement is always fulfilled by the default mutator that add a default connection pooling configuration if none is specified). Then there is the postgres-util sidecar that is a container only needed to execute administrative task directly on postgresql (this is the only on/off container without additional quirks).

Probably we could abstract better the cluster configuration if we remove completely the `sidecars` field. An user will be probably more comfortable with specific fields for each functionality he/she wants to enable/disable and configure. To achieve this we could just add two field for the only two functionality that could be actually configured by the `sidecars` field:

```
apiVersion: stackgres.io/v1alpha1
kind: StackGresCluster
metadata:
  name: <string>
spec:
  instances: <integer>
  pgVersion: <string>
  pgConfig: <string>
  connectionPooling: <boolean>

  resourceProfile: <string>
  backupConfig: <string>

    downloadDiskConcurrency: <integer>
  volumeSize: <string>
  storageClass: <string>
  postgresUtilContainer: <boolean>
  nonProduction:
    disableClusterPodAntiAffinity: <boolean>
```

Note that the part relevant to connection pooling is a bit redundant since require to set the flag to enable/disable connection pooling (`connectionPooling`) and the configuration name (`connectionPoolingConfig`). This is required in order to avoid to specify a connection pooling configuration and pick the default one while actually enabling connection pooling.

Could be interesting, internally, for StackGres, to generate the clusters without monitoring for centralized logging.

As per the `util` container, in the future we will end up using [ephemeral containers](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/ephemeral-containers/) where supported, as that's a much better option for this. As for now, we may do what you suggest, expose them as a boolean config that I'd name `postgresUtilContainer`.

I have no issues with the duality of the boolean config and the reference to the setting for the connection pooling, I would keep it as is.

[teoincontatto]: The `exporter` has been made as non-optional to use it in the UI (see #239).

delete subcommands:

Issue:
Backup configuration stored in backups could be different from used one
Backups uses wal-g configuration present in the master container in order to perform the backup. If backup configuration is changed but the master node does not apply it (currently this is only possible by restarting the master Pod) than the configuration used to perform the backup could be different from the configuration stored in the backup. This could lead to unrecoverable backups.

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: Not an easy problem to solve. I'll try to write down here possible solution and downsides of each one (if I can think of any):

1. Store backup configuration in the Pods. This is by copying backup configuration in some annotation field that get copied from the statefulset. The backup Job will read configuration from the master Pod and store it in the status of the backup CR that is being performed. 

This solution is hard to implement since currently the backup Job run with a script executed in a stripped container with just busybox and kubectl. The difficulty reside in parsing the annotation in JSON format. Probably this could be solved by including jq in the container.

2. Prevent backup from running if the backup configuration has not being applied in the master Pod. This could be done by storing the `resourceVersion` of the backup configuration in the Pod and prevent backup from running if the current backup configuration's `resourceVersion` is different from the one stored in the master Pod.

This is actually not the best solution since modifying the backup configuration should not stop at all backup from happening.

3. Generate wal-g configuration in by replacing wal-g environemnt variables in `kubectl exec` command sent from the backup job.

This solution could lead to WALs being stored with a backup configuration and backups with another making the backup restore misbehave by not restoring the latest changes.

Issue:
Fix backup reconciliation for backup CR deletion
Currently backup reconciliation is done using the latest backup configuration. Backup generated with a different backup storage configuration are not seen when reconciliation is executed. A workaround implemented in !159 prevent deletion of those backup CRs. Also if a cluster is deleted or the primary is not available reconciliation will not be executed at all.

We should convert reconciliation into a separate job possibly executed by a [finalizer](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/access-kubernetes-api/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#finalizers).

It is worth to convert the whole unmaintenable `create-backup.sh` script into a separate module of StackGres Java project (see #377).

[DISCUSSION]
[ahachete]: "Backup reconciliation" just means keeping the window of base backups current, right? I.e., if I want to keep always a sliding window of 5 base backups.

If so, I'd say that when the cluster is deleted and/or the configuration is changed, it is more than fine to keep previous backups out of this window. It is a small, almost desirable, problem to have more backups. Of course, it should be possible to delete them manually, but it suffices to me to simply keep them and not "re-introduce" them into the sliding window, since they come from a different config or a different cluster. So I'd say "no action required here".

What I agree is the refactor into a Java project and considerations about the finalizer.

[teoincontatto]: "Backup reconciliation" meaning is similar to "cluster reconciliation" in the reconciliation cycle of StackGres operator (with the difference that we can not recreate a backup that has been removed). The "backup reconciliation" takes all the existing real backups and all the existing backup CR and reconcile them by creating new real backups if a backup CR is created, updating them if the CR is updated, deleting real backups if the backup CR no longer exists and delete a backup CR if the real backup is deleted by retention process (or by the user).

A backup CR whose backup configuration is no longer used by the cluster will not be deleted by retention process. This backup CR can be deleted but the real backup will not be removed. Those "orphan" backup CRs (using double quote here because we see as orphan since the reconciliation process have no info about them but the real backup could actually be there) does not participate in the retention process so we are fine with them in this aspect.

If you still agree in that we are fine with "orphan" backup CR like they are right now them we could start a separate issue to move "backup reconciliation" to a Java implementation.

[ahachete]: OK, I understand and agree with the reconciliation principle here, the "sync" between the CR and a real backup.

However, I'm not quite sure we're 100% on the same page. I was thinking more of the concept of the backup configuration, where if you have a retention window of 5, but 4 existing backups from a previous backup config, none of those 4 will be deleted, and you may end up with a total of 9 backups. This is OK for me.

I don't see, however, that we should "orphan" backups. Every existing backup should have a representation as a CR, and vice-versa. Deletion of a CR should trigger the deletion of the backup, and vice-versa. Here, yes, there should be strong reconciliation, IMO.

[teoincontatto]: In that case I think we should let this issue be implemented to prevent "orphan" backups.

[ahachete]: ACK

Issue:
Use an appropriate storageClass as a default
Currently, if StackGresCluster.storage_class is not set, the default "`standard`" value is set. This was done under the (wrong) assumption that all or most environments had such a storage class by default. The reality is that most K8s environments have one storage class by default, but some have more, and in any case they have different names that are not "`standard`".

We must decide what do to among the following options:
1. Reject clusters without an explicit `storage_class` value (make it compulsory). Undesirable, as we tend to favor convention over configuration. Would make demos and one-command installs more complicated.
1. Create environment-dependent code to detect which cloud or on-prem environment we're present on, and have internal knowledge of the default names for the SCs on these environments. Prone to failure and requieres environment-dependent code.
1. Query dynamically existing SCs. If none is present, then error. If one is present, choose that one. If more than one is present, pick one as a default. In this case we may use alphabetic order as a second choice criteria and as a first choice criteria the SC whose name includes the string `ssd`, if any, to match higher-performing SCs which might be more appropriate for a database.

[DISCUSSION]
[ahachete]: I'd go for the third option.

[teoincontatto]: Let's use a 4th option. Taken from the minio helm chart:

>  minio data Persistent Volume Storage Class
>  If defined, storageClassName: <storageClass>
>  If set to "-", storageClassName: "", which disables dynamic provisioning
>  If undefined (the default) or set to null, no storageClassName spec is
>    set, choosing the default provisioner.  (gp2 on AWS, standard on
>    GKE, AWS & OpenStack)

So the `""` seem to already be the standard value (and not `"standard"` that is a standard in some kubernetes cluster deployments). This can also be checked in the official k8s docs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/#class-1

[ahachete]: OK, agreed, that's very good, but I believe the best link that explains this is https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/admission-controllers/#defaultstorageclass:

>  This admission controller observes creation of PersistentVolumeClaim objects that do not request any specific storage class and automatically adds a default storage class to them. This way, users that do not request any special storage class do not need to care about them at all and they will get the default one.

[ahachete]: Verified (on microk8s, as an example) that *not* setting the `storageClass` leads to usage of the default storage class on this environment:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: myclaim
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 8Gi
```

```
$ kubectl get pvc
NAME                  STATUS    VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS        AGE
myclaim               Bound     pvc-21e006fa-93fc-40d8-9833-9055add90bae   1Gi        RWO            microk8s-hostpath   6s
```

But I believe it is not `""` (empty, but non-null) string what we can use. This means do not use dynamic provisioning.

Still needs to be tested what happens on environments with multiple storage class.

[teoincontatto]: Absolutely agree on using null (or unset) as default value. This seems to be the standard approach for helm chart I could find around (like the minio one I mentioned before).

### Summary

On creation of new replicas on an existing cluster it will start new pods and hit a timeout of the liveness health check of Kubernetes so the pod it's restarted in a loop since the new replica never ends and patroni don't report success to Kubernetes.

* https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/kubernetes-best-practices-setting-up-health-checks-with-readiness-and-liveness-probes

* Create a cluster of 3 instances, create a database and populate with some data.
* Scale the instances to 5, it will create new pods and start creating the replica.
* Kubernetes will check the health of patroni, since it will create a new replica this will be a long operation and kubernetes will hit the timeout of the readyness and restart the pod in a loop.

Issue:
Allow scale down stackgres statefulset preventing the disruption of primary
Following discussion at https://gitlab.com/ongresinc/stackgres/issues/78#note_223832053

Currently, when using statefulset or other applications that manage a cluster of pods and allow to perform scale down, there is no way to prevent a particular pod from being disrupted. The topic is discussed in this kubernetes issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/45509

A workaround (as explained in the note above) is to extract the pod from the statefulset by changing label `disruptible` from `true` to `false`. This has to be done before updating the replicas number in the statefulset if the index number of the pod that has the label `role` with value `master` is equals or greater than the replicas number in the statefulset. The label `disruptible` have to change from `false` to `true` whenever the index number of the pod that has the label `role` with value `master` is less than the replicas number in the statefulset.

The label must change before changing the replicas number in statefulset.

[DISCUSSION]
[teoincontatto]: Ideally the label should be changed by patroni together with the role label. Research if that is possible and implement solution that way.

### Problem to solve

There is a concern that one Pod or Container could monopolize all of the resources.

By default, containers run with unbounded compute resources on a Kubernetes cluster. StackGres containers must have defined limit in memory and resources to be used from the cluster.

### Proposal

Create specification templates that can be linked to the StackGres cluster Custom Resource, this will assign the limits based on already defined templates or by allowing the use of custom specification templates.

| ------ | ------ | ----- | ----- |
| size-xs | 1 CPU | 1 GB | 10 GB  |
| size-s | 1 CPU | 2 GB | 25 GB | 
| size-m | 2 CPU | 4 GB | 38 GB | 
| size-l | 4 CPU | 8 GB | 115 GB  | 
| size-xl | 6 CPU | 16 GB | 270 GB | 
| size-xxl | 8 CPU | 32 GB | 580 GB | 

The connections limit is based on the RAM, for each GB of RAM it will allow 25 connections minus 3 reserved connections. Since a key component of StackGres will be a connection pooler, the connections limit can be reevaluated later.

NOTE: This limits are for each container that has the postgres cluster, for a 3 instance cluster that means using 3 times the resources of the profile (ex.: Profile S, 4GBx3 = 12GB) since the replicas will have the same configuration as the primary server.
